finding: A randomised controlled trial found that allowing early-2025 AI coding tools made experienced open-source developers 19% SLOWER on repositories they already knew well, and the same research group's late-2025 rerun reversed the point estimate to a speedup while the confidence intervals still straddle zero.
evidence: 16 developers completed 246 randomised tasks (2.0 hours on average) on repositories averaging 23,000 GitHub stars on which they had ~5 years of prior experience; AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer, confidence interval +2% to +39% | Participants forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still estimated a 20% speedup afterwards; economics experts predicted 39% shorter and ML experts 38% shorter | METR's late-2025 rerun (57 developers: 10 returning plus 47 newly recruited) estimates -18% (CI -38% to +9%) for returning developers and -4% (CI -15% to +9%) for new ones | METR reports 30% to 50% of developers withheld tasks they did not want to attempt without AI, and is redesigning the experiment because of that selection effect
old_way: Build-cost and schedule assumptions set from engineers' self-reported sense of how much faster AI makes them.
new_way: A randomised, time-measured comparison on real issues in real repositories, re-run as models improved, with the confidence interval published alongside the point estimate.
so_what: The only published RCT of AI coding tools on mature codebases found the developers' own perception wrong in direction, not just magnitude - so any BUILD business case in this organisation that rests on an engineering survey is resting on the exact measurement that failed; and the honest 2026 read is not '19% slower' but 'the effect is somewhere between a large speedup and a small slowdown, and nobody has measured yours'.
verification_note: Paper PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF; 16 developers, 246 tasks, 23,000-star average, 19% slowdown, 24% forecast, 20% post-hoc, 39%/38% expert forecasts all confirmed verbatim. CORRECTED vs source slice: slice said repositories averaged 22k+ stars (that is the blog's phrasing; the paper says 23,000 average) and reported NO confidence interval - the interval (+2% to +39%) appears only in METR's Feb 2026 update page, which was fetched. CORRECTED vintage: the slice presented the 19% slowdown as the current state; METR's own follow-up reverses the sign, and presenting the 2025 figure alone in 2026 would be a material vintage error. Graded B not A: arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. METR is an independent AI-evaluations nonprofit with no commercial stake in coding tools, but it does have an institutional interest in AI-capability scepticism. Authors state the result is specific to experienced developers on familiar mature codebases and does not generalise.

finding: In a randomised controlled trial that Google ran on its own engineers with its own internal tooling, AI assistance cut time on a complex enterprise-grade task by about 21%, with the authors stating the confidence interval is large.
evidence: 96 full-time Google software engineers randomised across three internal AI features on a complex, enterprise-grade task | Best estimate ~21% reduction in time on task, controlling for factors known to influence developer time | Authors state verbatim that the confidence interval is large and that the effect cannot be assumed to apply more broadly | Engineers who spend more hours per day on code-related activities were faster with AI; tooling was Google-internal as of summer 2024
old_way: Vendor-supplied or survey-based productivity estimates used as the basis for engineering tooling investment.
new_way: The employer runs its own randomised trial on its own engineers and its own stack, and publishes the caveat alongside the number.
so_what: A firm that wants a defensible engineering-productivity number can generate one in-house with 96 people and a randomisation script - which removes the excuse that the effect is unmeasurable, and means any leader still quoting a vendor percentage has chosen not to measure.
verification_note: arXiv abstract page re-fetched this run; 96 engineers, three AI features, ~21% and the phrase about a large confidence interval all appear verbatim. Graded B not A: the interval's bounds are never stated, so precision is unknown, and the study is an arXiv preprint (a slice note claims ICSE 2025 industry-track acceptance; that was NOT independently confirmed in this run). Google has a direct commercial interest in AI developer tooling. Vintage: summer-2024 internal tooling, a full model generation behind 2026 agents.

finding: On a small greenfield task with no existing codebase, freelance professional programmers with GitHub Copilot finished 55.8% faster than a no-AI control, with the largest gains going to the least experienced developers - the opposite experience gradient from the mature-codebase trial.
evidence: 95 professional programmers recruited via Upwork, randomised to Copilot or no-AI control, experiment run 15 May to 20 June 2022 just before Copilot's general availability | Treated group averaged 71.17 minutes to completion vs 160.89 minutes for control: a 55.8% reduction, p=0.0017, 95% confidence interval 21% to 89% | Task was implementing an HTTP server in JavaScript from scratch; control could still use internet search and Stack Overflow | Developers with less programming experience, older programmers, and those coding more hours per day benefited most
old_way: Treating AI coding gains as a single organisation-wide multiplier applied uniformly to all engineers and all work.
new_way: Effect size that swings from +56% to -19% depending on task novelty and how well the engineer already knows the codebase, making the moderator - not the tool - the thing to manage.
so_what: The headline number everybody quotes comes from writing an HTTP server from scratch on a freelance platform in 2022 - if your engineering roadmap is mostly extending systems you already own, you are buying the wrong study's number, and the same evidence base says the biggest wins go to your most junior people, not your most expensive ones.
verification_note: CORRECTED: the sample size (95), the 95% CI [21%,89%] and p=0.0017 do NOT appear on the arXiv abstract page the source slice cited as verification; the slice's second citation was an aggregator mirror (alphaxiv), which the brief's prune list excludes. PDF downloaded and extracted locally with PyMuPDF - all four figures plus the 71.17 vs 160.89 minute means confirmed verbatim. DOWNGRADED A to C: co-authors are from GitHub/Microsoft Research, i.e. the vendor whose product is being evaluated, which the evidence bar treats as sponsor interest; also an arXiv preprint. Vintage: 2022-era Copilot, pre-agentic, so this is a floor from an older model generation.

finding: In DORA's 2025 global survey, AI adoption turned positive for software delivery throughput and product performance but remained negatively associated with delivery stability, with the report framing AI as an amplifier of whatever engineering discipline already exists.
evidence: Nearly 5,000 technology professionals surveyed worldwide plus over 100 hours of qualitative interviews; published September 2025 | The 2025 report finds a positive relationship between AI adoption and both delivery throughput and product performance, reversing the prior year's finding | The negative relationship between AI adoption and delivery stability continues, tied to change volume outrunning automated testing and version-control maturity | 90% of respondents use AI at work and over 80% believe it raised their own productivity, while 30% report little or no trust in AI-generated code
old_way: Throughput and stability treated as co-moving symptoms of team maturity, tracked without reference to AI tool adoption.
new_way: Throughput and stability decouple under AI: shipping accelerates while change-failure and rework rise unless testing and version-control discipline is already strong.
so_what: The same dataset that supports the speed pitch also shows the defect and rework cost, and which side you land on is determined by your existing engineering hygiene rather than by the tool - so a stakeholder who owns the incident and rework budget should demand that any AI coding rollout be gated on test-automation maturity, not on licence count.
verification_note: CORRECTED STATISTIC: the source slice reported 'only ~30% report HIGH trust in AI-generated code'. The fetched page says the opposite construction - 30% report LITTLE OR NO trust in AI-generated code, slightly lower than the previous year. The inverted reading has been removed. Sample (~5,000 respondents, 100+ hours of interviews), 90% usage and 80%+ self-reported productivity confirmed on the Google Cloud page. dora.dev re-fetched and confirms Google Cloud as publisher with IT Revolution as premier partner and GitHub, GitLab, SkillBench and Workhelix as research partners - every one of which sells into AI developer tooling; sponsor interest is direct. Capped at B: these are self-reported survey correlations, not experimentally isolated causal estimates, and respondents self-select. The 80%+ self-reported productivity figure is not used as standalone support anywhere in this set.

finding: JPMorgan Chase has put AI coding assistants in front of more than 40,000 engineers and runs roughly 100 generative-AI solutions in production, but its own 2025 Investor Day deck reports no measured productivity effect from any of it - the only public number, 10-20%, comes from a CIO press interview with no disclosed method.
evidence: 2025 Investor Day deck, p13 (plain text, not a chart): over 200,000 users of LLM Suite, ~100 GenAI solutions in production, 40K+ engineers with AI coding assistants, ~80% of applications running largely on modern infrastructure (from ~75% last year) and ~65% largely in public or private cloud (from ~50%) | The same deck contains no measurement of what those coding assistants did to engineering output | Global CIO Lori Beer told Reuters (13 March 2025) that tens of thousands of engineers increased productivity 10% to 20% using the bank's own coding-assistant tool, with no sample, method, baseline or measurement window disclosed | Reuters reports JPMorgan's technology workforce at about 63,000 people, roughly a fifth of global headcount, with a 2024 technology budget of $17 billion
old_way: Engineering AI progress reported to the board as a tool-adoption census: seats deployed, users onboarded, solutions shipped.
new_way: Adoption at genuine scale in a systemically important bank - with the measurement of its effect on output still missing from the primary disclosure.
so_what: The largest US bank can tell you exactly how many engineers hold the tool and cannot tell its own investors what the tool did to output; if your AI engineering programme reports the same way, you have bought a deployment statistic and called it a return, and the 10-20% figure circulating internally probably traces to one executive interview rather than to a measurement anyone ran.
verification_note: 153-page Investor Day PDF re-downloaded and extracted locally with PyMuPDF this run; every p13 figure confirmed verbatim as body text rather than chart labels. Reuters-syndicated article re-fetched; Lori Beer quote, the 10-20% range, 63,000 technology staff and the $17bn 2024 technology budget confirmed. Merged from two inputs (a slice row resting only on press syndication, plus the orchestrator's verified recovery extract). The deployment census is A-grade primary disclosure; the 10-20% productivity range is C-grade single-source executive commentary with no method - the row is graded B overall and deliberately foregrounds the gap between the two. The deck is a marketing-grade investor presentation, not audited financial-statement content.

finding: JPMorgan's Consumer and Community Banking segment discloses a two-year engineering improvement - over 70% more code deployments, roughly 20% less requirement churn, over 30% fewer critical tech incidents - and pointedly does NOT attribute any of it to AI, which sits in a separate bullet on the same slide.
evidence: 2025 Investor Day p45 (slide 20), under the heading Strategic Investment and Product, Design, Analytics: over 70% more code deployments over the last 2 years, ~20% reduction in churn over the last 2 years, over 30% reduction in critical tech incidents - three separate bullets, of which only a fourth (a 35% year-on-year increase in value from AI/ML) mentions AI at all | Footnote 2 to slide 20 defines churn as unplanned changes to requirements during an agile sprint, tracked April to March | Footnote 3 states the 'over 2 return on investment with under 5 year payback' claim is based on FORECASTED multi-year returns for 2025 strategic tech investment, not realised returns | CCB Technology and Product expense ran $4.5B (2019) to $8.5B (2024) to ~$9B (2025 outlook), a 14% CAGR now moderating to 6% year on year
old_way: Engineering progress reported as velocity or story points, with AI credited for whatever improved in the same period.
new_way: A named, footnoted lifecycle metric - unplanned requirement change inside a sprint - reported on a fixed April-to-March basis, with the AI contribution kept in its own bullet rather than folded into the headline.
so_what: A bank with every incentive to claim an AI win instead published its engineering gains and its AI bullet as separate lines, and labelled its ROI figure as forecast; if your own AI business case would not survive that separation, the gain you are reporting may belong to cloud migration, platform work or a hiring cycle - and requirement churn, not code volume, is the number that actually tells you whether the front of the lifecycle is working.
verification_note: PDF extracted locally with PyMuPDF; p45 bullets and p77 (slide 52) footnotes 2 and 3 confirmed verbatim this run, and the orchestrator's recovery pass additionally rendered pp45-46 to images to confirm label-to-number pairing because slide text extraction scrambles reading order. Graded B not A: the deck does not attribute these metrics to AI, so the AI linkage is an absence-of-claim finding rather than a measured one, and the ROI figure is explicitly forward-looking. Scope caveat: slides 20-21 are Consumer and Community Banking only and must not be presented as firmwide. RELATED CORRECTION carried from the recovery pass: the widely repeated 'over 40% productivity versus 2024' operations figure is an ILLUSTRATIVE 5+ year forward target on p46, not an achieved result - the achieved figure is ~15% productivity versus 2019 - and the $19.8B 2026 technology budget figure does not appear in this deck at all.

finding: Under a CFPB no-action letter, Upstart's machine-learning underwriting model approved 27% more applicants at 16% lower average APRs than a traditional non-ML benchmark over 22 months - a result the CFPB published but explicitly declined to replicate or endorse.
evidence: CFPB blog, 6 August 2019: the tested model 'approves 27% more applicants than the traditional model, and yields 16% lower average APRs for approved loans' | CFPB describes the comparator as 'a hypothetical model that uses traditional application and credit file variables and does not employ machine learning', measured over a 22-month period | CFPB states verbatim that 'the simulations and analyses were not separately replicated by the Bureau' and that the letter 'does not serve as an endorsement of the use of any particular variables or modeling techniques' | Upstart's FY2021 Form 10-K: 'Variables in our AI models have increased from 23 in 2014 to more than 1,500 as of December 31, 2021'
old_way: Credit decisions built on a small set of traditional credit-file and application variables run through fixed rules.
new_way: A model carrying 1,500+ variables including education and employment signals, issuing both the approve/decline and the price, with the regulator publishing the results under a supervised no-action process.
so_what: This is the most-cited number in AI credit and its baseline is a hypothetical model the lender built itself, with the regulator on record refusing to replicate it - if this row is the strongest evidence your underwriting business case leans on, the case is weaker than it reads, and the durable lesson is the supervised-disclosure mechanism rather than the 27%.
verification_note: Both URLs re-fetched this run; the 27%, 16%, 22-month, non-replication and non-endorsement language confirmed verbatim on the CFPB page, and the 23-to-1,500 variable sentence confirmed verbatim in the 10-K. The 27/16 figures are Upstart's own simulations reported by the CFPB, not audited or replicated, and are specific to Upstart's applicant pool. The 10-K's separate claim of almost 75% lower loss rates versus 'several large U.S. banks' is EXCLUDED here: the banks are unnamed, which the evidence bar treats as unverifiable for a quantified claim. Vintage and technology caveat: 2019, and this is gradient-boosted predictive ML, not generative AI - it should not be presented as evidence of the current capability frontier. Jurisdiction: US.

finding: A model trained on delivery-app transaction data let RappiCard Mexico underwrite applicants with no credit history at an AUC of 0.791, and in 2025 it ran at a similar approval rate to the bank's old rules with half the default - with the lift coming almost entirely from proprietary transaction data rather than generic digital-footprint signals.
evidence: NBER Working Paper 33208: benchmark model achieves AUC 0.791 on applicants with no formal credit history, above the 0.6/0.7 desirability thresholds and at the upper end of alternative-data AUCs in middle-income countries | Footnote 4 verbatim: 'In 2025, the approval rate of the two models was very similar but the machine learning model with alternative data resulted in half as much default as the parsimonious rules' | Removing the delivery-app transactions data drops AUC by 0.137 (to 0.654), leaves the model only 31.4% as profitable, and cuts the profit-maximising approval rate from 69.4% to 49.5%; removing generic digital-footprint data costs only 0.014 of AUC | Verbatim: 'after testing a model similar to our default model beginning in September 2024, they now apply it to roughly half of applicants with no credit history'
old_way: Parsimonious manually-set rule cutoffs for applicants the credit bureau cannot score at all.
new_way: A model underwriting the no-file population off the parent platform's own purchase history, running live on about half of that population alongside the legacy rules.
so_what: The value is in the proprietary transaction stream, not in 'alternative data' as a category - generic digital-footprint signals bought a rounding error - so any institution planning to buy its way into this capability from a data vendor is buying the 0.014 and not the 0.137, and the same-lender same-population production comparison here is the evidence standard your own pilots should be held to.
verification_note: PDF re-downloaded and extracted locally with PyMuPDF this run (WebFetch returns raw binary); AUC 0.791, footnote 4's half-as-much-default sentence, the 0.137 AUC drop, 31.4% profitability, 69.4% vs 49.5% approval rates, the 0.014 digital-footprint contribution and the September 2024 production sentence all confirmed verbatim. Capped at B: NBER circulates working papers explicitly as not peer-reviewed. Funding disclosed in the paper's acknowledgements includes USAID, Gates-Foundation-linked CEGA/DCO and UC Berkeley LIFT; authors had data access from the lender. Jurisdiction: Mexico, a thin-file market - US/EU fair-lending constraints on using platform transaction data are materially tighter and this does not transfer unexamined. Paper revised April 2026, so the deployment share may have moved.

finding: JPMorgan Chase publishes six families of synthetic financial datasets so models can be built without real customer data, and an independent 2025 study using its public synthetic AML dataset produced a graph model that performed worse than a coin flip until real-world country data was added back in.
evidence: JPMorgan Chase's synthetic-data research page documents six dataset families - AML traces, retail customer-journey events, limit-order-book market data, payments with fraud labels, synthetic documents, and synthetic equity-market data - each with a named generation method and methodology citation, and states no quantified comparison of synthetic-trained versus real-data-trained model performance | Independent study (arXiv 2509.18499, Sept 2025) trained a relational graph convolutional network on JPMorgan's public synthetic AML dataset: 523,877 transactions across 16 countries, 20% labelled fraudulent | Result verbatim: 'Our model's AUC value of 43.64% indicates that it performed worse than a coin flip', with an F1-score of 7.75% | After adding four real-world country-level indicators (Basel AML Index, Tufts Digital Evolution Index, Corruption Perceptions Index, GDP per capita): accuracy 64.93% to 83.39%, F1 7.75% to 59.37%, AUC 43.64% to 74.63%
old_way: Model development throttled by privacy and confidentiality restrictions on access to real customer, AML and trading data.
new_way: Published synthetic datasets stand in for real data during early development - but, on the one public test available, only once real-world contextual features are blended back in.
so_what: 'Synthetic data removes the data-access blocker' is the premise behind a large share of AI build roadmaps in regulated firms, and the only independent utility test on a major bank's own published synthetic dataset found the synthetic-only model unusable - so the right question to ask a team proposing synthetic data is not whether the data is realistic but what the model scores against a real-data holdout.
verification_note: Merged from two source rows. arXiv PDF downloaded and extracted with PyMuPDF; all six figures (43.64, 7.75, 64.93, 83.39, 59.37, 74.63), the 523,877-transaction / 16-country / 20%-fraudulent dataset description and the 'worse than a coin flip' sentence confirmed verbatim. JPMorgan page re-fetched; the six dataset families and the absence of any synthetic-vs-real performance comparison confirmed. CORRECTED: the source slice stated the equity-market dataset uses 'machine learning trained on historical Bloomberg data'; the page describes training on historical spot and option prices and does not name Bloomberg - the attribution has been removed. The JPMorgan page is undated and maintained on a rolling basis; source_date reflects the arXiv study, which carries the load-bearing numbers. The arXiv paper is a preprint, not peer-reviewed; authors are at William and Mary, University of Alabama and CGI Federal, with no funding or conflict statement found. Caveat: this tests one public synthetic dataset with one model architecture - it is not a general verdict on synthetic data.

finding: DBS's FY2024 annual report discloses 1.2 billion AI-generated personalised nudges delivered to more than 13 million customers in one year, at a scale no human relationship-management model could reach, with the customer-outcome multiples resting on an engaged-versus-non-engaged comparison rather than a holdout.
evidence: DBS FY2024 annual report: more than 1.2 billion personalised nudges to more than 13 million customers across the region | Over 1,500 models running across more than 370 use cases | AI/ML initiatives delivered over SGD 750 million of economic value in 2024, more than double the previous year | In Singapore, customers who engaged with nudges and the AI financial-planning tool 'saved two times more, invested five times more and were nearly three times more insured than non-users'
old_way: Segment-level campaign calendars and periodic relationship-manager outreach, with personalisation limited by how many conversations humans can have.
new_way: Continuously generated, individually targeted in-app prompts at a volume of roughly 90 messages per customer per year, with value tracked as a bank-wide AI/ML line.
so_what: A bank has already moved the launch channel from campaign-to-segment to message-to-individual at a billion-message scale, which resets what 'personalised' means in any competitive comparison - but note that DBS reports its lift by comparing customers who engaged against those who did not, which is the same self-selected comparison your own marketing team probably uses, and it is not causal.
verification_note: Page re-fetched this run; the SGD 750m, 1,500 models, 370 use cases, 1.2 billion nudges, 13 million customers and the 2x/5x/3x sentence all confirmed verbatim. The SGD 750m figure covers all bank-wide AI/ML initiatives, NOT nudges alone, and must not be presented as personalisation ROI. The 2x/5x/3x multiples compare self-selected engaged users with non-engaged users - correlational, not a randomised holdout. Nudge and reach figures are pan-regional; the outcome multiples are Singapore-only. Graded B not A: these are unaudited operating metrics inside an annual report, not financial-statement content, and no independent verification of any figure was found. Survivorship caveat: this is DBS's own success narrative in its own report.

finding: Lemonade's FY2025 Form 10-K states that its conversational AI and APIs sell 98% of its policies and that AI takes first notice of loss without human intervention 96% of the time - an entire distribution and intake channel handed to an agentic interface, disclosed in an SEC filing rather than a press release.
evidence: FY2025 Form 10-K verbatim: 'AI Maya and our APIs sell 98% of Lemonade's policies' | Verbatim: 'As of December 31, 2025, 96% of the time, it is AI Jim that will take the first notice of loss from a Lemonade customer without human intervention' | Verbatim: 'As of December 31, 2025, roughly 55% of our claims were automated, resulting in instant or near-instant processing from start to finish' | The filing describes AI Jim triaging complex cases to human claims experts by qualification and workload, so automation is routed rather than universal
old_way: Agent-mediated or long-web-form application, underwriting and claims intake, with human handling as the default path and automation as the exception.
new_way: A conversational agent runs the full quote-bind-issue dialogue and takes the loss notice, with humans retained as an escalation tier rather than the front line.
so_what: The debate over whether customers will transact through an AI interface is settled at one public insurer: 98% of its policies already sell that way, and it is in a 10-K - so the live question for an incumbent is not whether the channel works but whether your product complexity and legacy intake are the reason you cannot use it, which is an argument about your own architecture, not about AI.
verification_note: SEC EDGAR filing re-fetched this run; all three figures (98%, 96%, 55%) and the as-of date confirmed verbatim in the filing text. These are company-selected operating KPIs disclosed inside a filing - they carry filing liability but are not covered by the financial-statement audit opinion. Transferability caveat: Lemonade is a small AI-native insurer writing simple lines (renters, pet, home, some auto and life); these automation rates should not be assumed to carry to complex commercial, life or annuity underwriting at incumbents. Jurisdiction: US.

company: Citigroup | New York Life | TIAA | Vanguard | Blackstone
finding: Six separately regulated financial institutions have put their own capital into a single vendor building AI agents that pre-review marketing and sales material for compliance, and New York Life confirms a live partnership on that exact use case - but not one of them has disclosed a measured change in review turnaround.
evidence: Citi Ventures' own press release (26 June 2024) announces an investment in Norm Ai's Series A, describing agents that convert regulations into executable programs assessing compliance; it states users can 'move faster while remaining compliant and reducing costs' with no quantified metric | New York Life's own newsroom page (17 June 2025) confirms a live partnership currently focused on reviewing sales and marketing content, with CCO Sandi Tillotson joining Norm Ai's Regulatory Advisory Board and Alex Cook its AI Agent Advisory Committee; it says the platform is 'accelerating the review process' but discloses no numbers | Norm Ai's March 2025 funding release names Citi Ventures, New York Life Ventures, TIAA Ventures, Vanguard, Blackstone Innovations Investments, Bain Capital, Coatue, Craft Ventures and Marc Benioff in a $48m Series B, $87m raised over 18 months | Neither institution's own materials contain a before/after review-time figure
old_way: Sequential manual legal and compliance sign-off on every piece of customer-facing marketing content, sitting on the critical path to launch.
new_way: AI agents pre-screen content against codified regulatory rules before human sign-off, with regulated institutions funding and co-designing the tooling rather than buying a finished product.
so_what: Competing regulated institutions are spending their own balance sheet on the compliance-review bottleneck rather than on content generation, which tells you where they think launch time actually goes - and the fact that none of them will publish a turnaround number tells you the fix is not yet proven, so treat this as a read on where the constraint is, not as evidence it has been removed.
verification_note: All three pages re-fetched this run. CORRECTED: the source slice described the funding as 'Series A, ~$27M, June 2024' plus a 'further $48M round, March 2025'. The fetched release describes a $48m SERIES B dated 11 March 2025 with $87m raised in total over 18 months; the $27m Series A figure appears on none of the pages fetched and has been removed. Citi's page confirms the Series A investment but states no amount. Slice also said 'Bain Capital Ventures'; the release says Bain Capital. This row documents an adoption and investment pattern, NOT a measured outcome - no institution discloses a compliance-review-time metric, so per the evidence bar an announcement is not an outcome and maturity is PILOT. The investor list comes from the vendor's own press release, which is a vendor source; the two load-bearing facts (Citi's investment, New York Life's live marketing-review partnership) each come from that institution's own site. Survivorship caveat: firms that piloted AI compliance review and dropped it would not appear in this search.

finding: In a two-month randomised controlled trial on a financial-services app during the 2025 US tax-filing season, agent-led personalised messaging cut unsubscribe events by 21% against the firm's existing rule-based campaign system and pulled filing behaviour earlier in the window.
evidence: Abstract verbatim: 'agent-led messaging reduced unsubscribe events by 21% (plus or minus 0.01) relative to BAU' | Design: two-month randomised controlled trial against a business-as-usual rule-based campaign system, run on a financial-service application's customer communication system during a 2025 national tax-filing period | Second outcome: increased early filing behaviour in the weeks preceding the national deadline, with no separate effect size given in the abstract | Authors Olivier Jeunen and Schaun Wheeler, arXiv 2512.17462, December 2025
old_way: A fixed rule-based reminder cadence applied uniformly to a target segment, with list attrition treated as an unavoidable cost of campaigning.
new_way: An agent making per-customer decisions about message timing, content and intensity through the campaign window, with retention treated as a measured outcome alongside conversion.
so_what: This is one of the very few launch-messaging claims in the whole evidence set built on an actual randomised control with a reported interval - and the real effect is 21% on unsubscribes, an order of magnitude below the triple-digit lifts vendors quote, which is the honest size of gain to budget for; note also that the outcome it moved was retention of the audience, not conversion, which is not the metric most campaign dashboards report.
verification_note: Abstract page re-fetched this run; the 21% figure with its stated interval, the two-month RCT design, the BAU comparator and the early-filing direction all confirmed verbatim. arXiv preprint with no confirmed peer-review venue - PEER_REVIEWED is used only because the fixed vocabulary has no preprint option; treat as B-grade third-party research with a disclosed method. The financial-services firm is anonymised by the authors (normal for an industry RCT), so company is N/A. No institutional affiliation is stated on the abstract page, so independence from a vendor could not be confirmed - one author is associated with commercial personalisation tooling, which is an unresolved interest. The full paper's methodology section was not separately reviewed; the conversion-timing effect has no published effect size and is therefore reported as direction only.

finding: The Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC replaced SR 11-7, the 2011 guidance that underpins every US bank model-risk programme, with new interagency guidance issued 17 April 2026 that narrows its own primary scope to banking organisations above $30 billion in assets and defines 'model' so as to exclude deterministic rule-based software.
evidence: SR 26-2 cover letter, 17 April 2026: it 'supersedes and replaces SR letter 11-7, Guidance on Model Risk Management (April 4, 2011)' and SR 21-8 (April 9, 2021) | Cover letter: 'This letter is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets regulated by the Federal Reserve' | Guidance attachment p3: the term 'model' excludes 'simple arithmetic calculations, such as those found within spreadsheets, as well as deterministic rule-based processes and software where there are no statistical, economic, or financial theories underpinning their design or use' | Guidance attachment p3: banks at or below $30bn are 'generally excluding them from this guidance', though it 'may be relevant' where model-risk exposure is significant | OCC Bulletin 2026-13 of the same date confirms joint issuance by the OCC, Federal Reserve Board and FDIC
old_way: Compliance and product teams treat SR 11-7 (2011) as the permanent, universal baseline: any analytical system is a 'model', every bank is in scope, and validation and effective-challenge expectations are settled and known.
new_way: As of April 2026 the operative text is new, is primarily aimed at banks above $30bn, and carries a model definition that expressly leaves rule-based and non-theory-driven software outside it - so the first governance question is now whether a given tool is a 'model' at all, not how to validate it.
so_what: The stakeholder sentence 'we already comply with SR 11-7' now cites a document that was withdrawn in April 2026. Before any AI product decision is routed to model risk, the firm has to re-answer two questions the old framework had settled: is this thing a model under the new definition, and is our institution inside the guidance's primary scope. That re-scoping work is a launch dependency that should be started now, not discovered at the review gate.
verification_note: Cover letter fetched this run; guidance attachment downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF (12 pages) and all quoted language read directly from page 3 of the extracted text. OCC bulletin fetched independently and carries identical scope language, so the fact is corroborated across two agencies. The cover letter itself makes no mention of AI - a verifier reading only the cover letter would wrongly conclude the guidance is silent on AI scope; see GOVERN-02. Vintage-critical: any source published after April 2026 describing SR 11-7 as current Fed model-risk guidance is out of date.

finding: Footnote 3 of the April 2026 interagency model-risk guidance places generative AI and agentic AI models outside its scope while expressly keeping traditional statistical models and non-generative, non-agentic AI inside it, and directs banks to govern the out-of-scope tools under their own risk-management practices pending a future request for information.
evidence: SR 26-2 guidance attachment, footnote 3, p3, verbatim: 'Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this guidance.' | Same footnote, verbatim: 'Nonetheless, a banking organization's risk management and governance practices should guide the determination of appropriate governance and controls for any tools, processes, or systems not covered in this document.' | Same footnote, verbatim: 'However, the principles described in this guidance apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI models.' | OCC Bulletin 2026-13: the agencies 'plan to issue in the near future a request for information that addresses model risk management generally and considers, in particular, banks' use of AI, including generative AI and agentic AI and AI-based models'
old_way: The reflexive objection that model risk management already covers AI: a model is a model, SR 11-7-style development, validation, monitoring and effective challenge were written broadly enough to absorb any new technique, so generative AI is simply the next thing to put through the existing gate.
new_way: The agencies themselves say the existing gate does not cover generative or agentic AI, keep predictive and traditional models firmly inside it, and hand the design of controls for the excluded category back to each bank's own risk-management function while they gather information.
so_what: This is a governance vacuum, not a governance wall, and it is emphatically not a permission slip. Two practical consequences for the lifecycle: first, 'model risk will block it' is not a defensible reason to stop a generative-AI product, because the guidance declines to cover it; second, the firm that designs its own defensible controls now is the one that will not have to retrofit when the RFI turns into expectations. The same footnote also means predictive credit and pricing models get no relief at all.
verification_note: Footnote 3 read verbatim from a local PyMuPDF text extraction of the Federal Reserve's own guidance attachment, and the same carve-out sentence independently confirmed on the OCC bulletin page fetched this run. The RFI is a stated plan, not an issued document - no RFI has been located, so nothing should be claimed about its content or timing. Deliberately stated with the in-scope half attached: presenting the carve-out alone would misrepresent a scope boundary as deregulation. Applies to US federal banking supervision only; state regulators, the CFPB and non-bank lenders are not covered.

finding: The CFPB withdrew Circular 2022-03, its interpretation that lenders cannot use complex algorithms they are unable to explain in adverse-action notices, on 12 May 2025, but the circular's own landing page still presents as active guidance and the underlying ECOA and Regulation B duty to give specific reasons is untouched.
evidence: CFPB withdrawn-guidance index, verbatim entry: 'Consumer Financial Protection Circular 2022-03: Adverse Action Notification Requirements in Connection With Credit Decisions Based on Complex Algorithms, 87 FR 35864 (June 14, 2022); withdrawn on May 12, 2025' | The circular's own page on consumerfinance.gov carries no withdrawal banner and reads as live guidance, which is a concrete reason practitioners still cite it as current | The withdrawn-guidance index makes no statement whatsoever about the legal effect of withdrawal on underlying obligations - the silence was checked for specifically | The circular is one of roughly one hundred documents listed as withdrawn across advisory opinions, interpretive rules, circulars and policy statements
old_way: Explainability programmes for credit models are justified internally by pointing at Circular 2022-03: the Bureau has said a black-box model is not an excuse, therefore reason codes must be produced, therefore opaque models are off the table.
new_way: The Bureau's interpretive gloss is gone, so the specific federal interpretation that named complex algorithms no longer exists - while the statutory requirement it was interpreting, ECOA's and Regulation B's demand for specific reasons for adverse action, remains fully in force and enforceable.
so_what: Do not let anyone in the room convert this into 'explainability is no longer required' - that is the single most damaging error available in this deck, because the statutory duty is unchanged and only the Bureau's commentary on it was withdrawn. What actually changed is the certainty: teams that built reason-code capability to match the 2022 circular now have less regulatory cover for their specific design choices, and teams still citing 2022-03 as live doctrine are planning against a withdrawn document whose web page does not tell them so.
verification_note: Withdrawal date read verbatim from the CFPB's own withdrawn-guidance index fetched this run; the circular's live page was fetched separately and confirmed to show no withdrawal notice. The Federal Register withdrawal notice itself could not be opened - federalregister.gov 302-redirects automated fetches to a CAPTCHA gate - so the issuing agency's own index is used instead, which is better provenance in any case. A count of 67 withdrawn documents appearing in an earlier draft could not be substantiated and was removed; the index as fetched lists roughly one hundred. No replacement CFPB guidance on algorithmic adverse action has been located, and which explainability techniques examiners will now accept is an open question, not settled practice.

finding: The EU AI Act classifies AI used to evaluate consumer creditworthiness and to price life and health insurance as high-risk under Annex III, but the European Commission now states those rules apply from 2 December 2027 following the AI Omnibus that entered into force on 27 July 2026.
evidence: European Commission digital-strategy page on the AI Omnibus, verbatim: 'High-risk AI systems in Annex III: Rules apply starting 2 December 2027' and 'High-risk AI embedded in physical products (machinery, toys, lifts, etc.) in Annex I: Rules apply starting 2 August 2028' | Same page, verbatim: 'On 27 July 2026, the AI Omnibus enters into force across the EU', described as 'proposed as part of the digital omnibus package on 19 November 2025' and as extending timelines and delivering 'targeted simplification of the AI rulebook while preserving strong safeguards' | The Commission's regulatory-framework page names 'credit scoring denying citizens opportunity to obtain a loan' as an example of high-risk access to essential private services | Annex III point 5(b) covers AI 'to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud'; point 5(c) covers 'risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance'
old_way: European credit and insurance product plans built around an August 2026 high-risk compliance date, with conformity assessment treated as an immediate blocking dependency on any AI-assisted underwriting or pricing work.
new_way: The classification stands but the clock moved: standalone Annex III systems including consumer credit scoring and life and health insurance pricing face the high-risk regime from 2 December 2027, with embedded product AI at 2 August 2028.
so_what: For a European or EU-facing credit or life and health insurance business this is roughly sixteen extra months of runway on the hardest compliance dependency in the lifecycle - which is an argument for building the conformity evidence trail into the next product cycle rather than an argument to defer it. Getting the date wrong in either direction, claiming it binds today or dismissing it as distant, is the fastest way to lose a regulator-literate room. Note the boundary: general property and casualty and commercial insurance pricing is not in Annex III point 5(c), only life and health.
verification_note: The orchestrator's verification memo confirmed the 2 December 2027 date but could not confirm the Digital Omnibus mechanism against the unofficial tracker and instructed that it be dropped unless confirmed on EUR-Lex or an official Commission page. It is confirmed here: both the date and the 27 July 2026 entry into force were read this run from the European Commission's own digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu pages, which also describe the package as extending timelines. Graded B rather than A because the verbatim Annex III 5(b) and 5(c) wording still rests on artificialintelligenceact.eu, an unofficial consolidated-text mirror: EUR-Lex returned zero bytes on two direct attempts (HTTP 202 bot gate) for both the HTML and PDF of Regulation 2024/1689, so the primary legal text was not read. No original 2 August 2026 date appears on the Commission pages fetched, so the size of the deferral is stated in the so_what as approximate and is not asserted as a quoted figure. EU jurisdiction only.

finding: In the Bank of England and FCA's November 2024 survey of 118 UK financial firms, formal AI accountability structures are far more widespread than actual understanding of the AI in use: 84% report a named accountable person for their AI framework while only 34% claim complete understanding of the AI technologies they deploy.
evidence: Survey, verbatim: '75% of firms are already using artificial intelligence (AI), with a further 10% planning to use AI over the next three years' | Verbatim: '46% of respondent firms reported having only partial understanding of the AI technologies they use versus 34% of firms that said they have complete understanding' | Verbatim: '84% of firms reported having an accountable person for their AI framework' | The survey received 118 responses and was published on 21 November 2024
old_way: A named senior accountable person and an AI governance committee are reported to boards as evidence that the AI estate is understood and under control, and are used to close the governance line item.
new_way: The supervisors' own data separates the two: accountability paperwork at 84% sits far ahead of complete technical understanding at 34%, with 46% conceding only partial understanding of systems already in production.
so_what: This is a supervisor-sourced answer to 'we already have AI governance in place' used as a reason to slow-walk product change. The same regulators who would examine the firm have published evidence that naming an accountable executive is not the same as understanding the estate - which reframes the governance investment from committee formation to technical comprehension, and makes independent assurance of deployed models a live budget question rather than a theoretical one.
verification_note: All four figures read verbatim from the Bank of England report page fetched this run. UK jurisdiction, not US - do not present to a US audience as domestic evidence; no comparable structured US supervisory AI-adoption survey was found, which is itself notable. Self-reported by firms to their supervisor, which cuts both ways: firms have an incentive to overstate governance maturity, so the 34% complete-understanding figure is if anything generous. Vintage: November 2024 fieldwork, so it predates the 2025-2026 agentic AI wave. A widely repeated secondary claim that 81% of AI-using firms use an explainability method, mostly SHAP, could not be found in the fetched text and is excluded rather than asserted.

finding: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile are described by NIST itself as intended for voluntary use and carry no certification or conformity-assessment scheme, so being NIST-aligned satisfies no binding US financial-services requirement on its own.
evidence: NIST, verbatim: 'The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is intended for voluntary use and to improve the ability to incorporate trustworthiness' | Verbatim: 'Released on January 26, 2023, the Framework was developed through a consensus-driven, open, transparent, and collaborative process' | Verbatim: 'On July 26, 2024, NIST released NIST-AI-600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile' | The NIST AI RMF page describes no certification, accreditation or conformity-assessment mechanism, and specifies no financial-services requirements
old_way: Vendor and consultancy materials present NIST alignment as a compliance credential - 'NIST-compliant AI governance' - and firms accept it as evidence that a regulatory obligation has been discharged.
new_way: NIST frames the RMF and its profiles as voluntary risk-management guidance with no audit or certification regime behind them: alignment is a defensible process posture a firm can show an examiner, not a requirement any examiner is checking against.
so_what: A precision correction worth making before the room does it for you. NIST alignment is a reasonable thing to claim and useful for demonstrating a documented process, but it is not a substitute for, or evidence of, compliance with the April 2026 interagency model-risk guidance, ECOA and Regulation B, or the EU AI Act. Conflating a voluntary framework with a binding one is exactly the imprecision that lets a regulatory-minded stakeholder dismiss a whole governance argument.
verification_note: Dates and the voluntary-use language read verbatim from nist.gov fetched this run. Two claims from an earlier draft were removed because they are not on the fetched page: that the Generative AI Profile explicitly 'does not replace the base framework', and a list of twelve generative-AI risk categories - both rested on secondary sources and NIST AI 600-1 itself was not fetched. The absence of a certification scheme is an absence of evidence on the page rather than an affirmative NIST statement that none exists; it is stated that way here.

finding: In the Census Bureau's 2023 Annual Business Survey, US businesses that adopted AI most often reported no overall change in their number of workers, and where headcount did move, increases were more common than decreases.
evidence: Census reporting on the 2023 Annual Business Survey: businesses said their 'number of workers did not change overall' after adopting AI between 2020 and 2022 | Across the technologies surveyed, 'all (except robotics) were reportedly more likely to increase than decrease worker numbers' | The adoption window covered is 2020 to 2022, from the 2023 Annual Business Survey which produced 2022 reference-year data | This is a nationally representative government business survey rather than a self-selected case-study set
old_way: Workforce planning and board narratives treat AI adoption as a leading indicator of near-term headcount reduction, and any single firm's cuts are read as confirmation of an economy-wide effect.
new_way: The most representative firm-level US evidence available shows adoption proceeding with no measured aggregate employment effect in the near term, and a skew toward headcount increases where any change occurred at all.
so_what: This is the base rate against which every operating-model claim in this deck should be read, including the bank-specific rows that follow. It does not say AI cannot reduce headcount; it says the population-level signal is not there yet, so any individual firm's headcount story needs its own attribution evidence rather than borrowing credibility from a general trend that the data does not show.
verification_note: Fetched from census.gov this run; the quoted phrasing appears in the fetched text. Vintage caveat that materially limits this row: the adoption window is 2020-2022, largely before the generative-AI capability frontier, so it may understate current effects - it is evidence about the pre-LLM adoption wave, not about 2026 agentic deployments. Firm-reported rather than administratively observed, though collected by a federal statistical agency with disclosed methodology. No finance-sector employment breakdown was published in the fetched page. A second Census page on 2026 adoption rates was moved to COUNTER-04 to avoid duplicating the same underlying survey across two rows.

finding: JPMorgan's consumer bank discloses roughly 15% operations productivity improvement from 2019 to 2024 on approximately flat operations headcount, and explicitly excludes Home Lending from the calculation because that unit's headcount fell for macroeconomic rather than technological reasons.
evidence: 2025 Investor Day deck, slide 21 (PDF p46), 2019 vs 2024 key performance metrics: accounts serviced per Operations headcount up 'more than 25%', servicing calls per account down 29%, processing cost per account down 15%, cost of fraud in basis points approximately flat, and operations headcount approximately flat | The illustrative chart pairs business growth of 28% with headcount growth of 13% by 2024, giving 'about 15% productivity vs. 2019' | Footnote 2 to slide 21 (PDF p52 of the deck, PDF p77), verbatim: 'Operations productivity excludes Home Lending, which has realized a meaningful headcount reduction due to the macro environment' | The 'more than 40% productivity vs. 2024' and 'down 10%' headcount figures on the same chart sit at its '5+ years' forward position, not at 2024
old_way: Operations headcount scales with account and transaction volume, so growth in the book of business has historically meant proportional growth in servicing staff, and productivity claims are asserted without disclosing which business units were included.
new_way: A named bank publishes a servicing productivity series with volume growth decoupled from headcount, and publishes the exclusion that makes the number honest - carving out the division where headcount fell for reasons unrelated to technology.
so_what: Two things for an operating-model conversation. First, the achievable, disclosed, already-banked number is around 15% over five years on flat headcount, not the 40% that circulates - that is the figure to plan against. Second, and more useful: this is a systemically important bank performing the attribution correction on itself in an investor document. It is the template for how to report an AI-era productivity number that will survive a sceptical reading, and it sets the standard any internal claim in your own firm should be held to.
verification_note: The 153-page deck was downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF this run; slide 21 and the footnote page were read directly and match the orchestrator's independent visual verification of the same pages. Graded B not A because the productivity figures are chart-embedded rather than body text, and because the deck does not attribute the operations productivity gain to AI specifically - the attribution boundary is left intact here deliberately. Figures are Consumer and Community Banking segment only and must not be presented as firmwide. Press-sourced figures from an earlier draft were dropped in favour of the primary document: a '10% headcount reduction' attributed to an executive is on this chart only as an illustrative 5+ year point, and the '317,000 employees' and '$18 billion technology budget' figures are not in this deck.

finding: Citigroup's programme to eliminate around 20,000 roles was unveiled in early 2024 as a management-delayering and cost exercise and is now being narrated by the CEO as a technology and process-simplification story, while the bank separately reports large-scale internal AI tool usage without connecting the two.
evidence: The restructuring was unveiled in early 2024 to simplify management layers, streamline businesses and deliver up to $2.5 billion in cost savings, targeting roughly 20,000 jobs or about 8% of the global workforce by 2026 | More than 10,000 roles had already been shed before January 2026, with about 1,000 more eliminated in January 2026 | CEO Jane Fraser in January 2026 framed further reductions around technology and process simplification meaning 'others will no longer be required', and told staff 'We are not graded on effort. We are judged on our results' | On the Q3 2025 earnings call Citi reported nearly 180,000 employees across 83 countries using its proprietary AI tools, and 'more than 1 million AI-driven automated code reviews this year, creating 100,000 hours of weekly capacity for developers'
old_way: A bank's headcount reduction is explained by the programme that actually produced it - in this case a 2024 cost and organisational-simplification plan with no AI framing at the time of announcement.
new_way: The same continuing reduction acquires an AI and automation narrative two years later, in the period when that framing is most rewarded by markets and most expected by boards, without the firm publishing an AI-attributable headcount figure.
so_what: Treat this as the live worked example of the attribution problem in your own operating-model reporting. The AI usage figures Citi discloses are real and large, and the headcount reduction is real and large, but the firm has published nothing connecting them - and the programme predates the generative-AI wave by two years. Before any internal efficiency number is credited to AI in your own deck, ask the same question: what was the programme called before AI was the answer.
verification_note: Both articles fetched this run and every figure above appears in the fetched text. Two corrections from an earlier draft: the restructuring announcement is dated early 2024 in the fetched source, not 2023 as previously stated, and an approximately $800 million full-year 2025 severance figure could not be found in either fetched article and has been removed. Trade and business press reporting of on-the-record statements and an earnings call, not a filed disclosure fetched directly. This row should not be read as evidence that AI caused the cuts - only that the company now narrates them that way, which is the point of including it.

finding: Wells Fargo has shed roughly 70,000 roles since late 2019 while its CEO publicly refuses to attribute the decline to AI, describing AI's employment effect as simultaneously job-creating and job-displacing and saying reductions are pursued through normal attrition.
evidence: Headcount fell from approximately 275,000 in late 2019 to approximately 205,000, and to about 201,000 as of Q1 2026 | At a Bernstein investor conference on 28 May 2026 CEO Charlie Scharf said of the job-creating versus job-displacing debate: 'I find it very surprising when really smart people take one side or the other... It's so obvious to me... it is both of those things' | Scharf, verbatim: 'People don't go away in this', and separately that 'The risk is that they're not totally aligned, in terms of the same people and the timing of it' | The bank aims to take reductions 'through normal attrition as we can', and Scharf said it is 'far from done. Not even close' on optimisation
old_way: A 70,000-role decline at a top-five US bank is reported and repeated as a single AI-driven workforce story, because that is the available narrative frame.
new_way: The chief executive decomposes it instead: a multi-year efficiency programme delivered largely through attrition, with AI's net employment effect described as genuinely two-sided and the timing and identity of affected people explicitly unresolved.
so_what: A second named bank declining to take the easy AI credit, and the most useful sentence in it for an operating-model discussion is Scharf's point that creation and displacement are 'not totally aligned, in terms of the same people and the timing of it'. That is the actual org-design problem - not a net headcount number, but a reskilling and sequencing problem inside a workforce that does not reshuffle on the same clock as the technology.
verification_note: Fetched this run; headcount figures and all quoted statements appear in the fetched text. Correction from an earlier draft: a CFO statement attributed to the Q3 2025 earnings call about the drivers of headcount decline does not appear in this article and has been removed, as has the claim of simultaneous hiring in AI and investment-banking roles, which is likewise not in the fetched text. Single-source, trade-press account of an on-the-record investor conference rather than a filed disclosure. The 2019-2026 decline spans pre-AI cost programmes, branch closures and pandemic-era changes, so no AI-attributable share is separable from this source and none should be inferred.

finding: A $64 billion-asset regional bank says AI-assisted development has shifted its build-versus-buy calculus far enough that it is replacing three external vendor contracts with internally built software, while deliberately rationing AI tool access to about 80 of 3,600 employees.
evidence: COO Russ Barrett, verbatim: 'We are already replacing three external contracts with our ability to leverage AI' | Valley Bank has $64 billion in assets and approximately 3,600 employees, of whom about 80 have unrestricted AI tool access as a cross-functional group of power users | The bank operates five tiers of employee AI access, two of them serving engineering, quality assurance and model risk management with specialised tools, the rest progressively restricted to prevent expensive custom agent development | Barrett said Valley reached production on AI-powered prospecting and fraud capabilities sooner than similarly sized banks working with the same AI partners, while conceding Valley may not lead on total use-case count
old_way: Midsize banks without large in-house engineering organisations default to buying point solutions for specific workflows, because building and maintaining software was not cost-effective below a certain scale.
new_way: AI-assisted engineering narrows the build cost gap enough that a regional bank insources workflow tools it previously bought - and pairs that with an explicit cost-control regime that rations who can build with AI at all.
so_what: The procurement implication is the sharp one: if the build-versus-buy line is moving at $64 billion in assets, every renewal of a workflow-specific vendor contract becomes a build decision that has to be actively made rather than assumed. The five-tier access scheme is the other half and is rarely discussed - unmetered AI access is itself a cost centre, and this bank treats access allocation as an operating-model decision.
verification_note: Fetched this run; all figures and the quotation appear in the fetched text. Correction from an earlier draft: the article is dated 10 July 2026, not September 2026, and the source_date is corrected accordingly. Downgraded from B to C: this is one executive's unverified account of his own bank's internal decisions, with no vendor named, no contract value disclosed and no confirmation that the three contracts were terminated rather than reduced, and no independent corroboration - it is a single data point, not a trend, and it exists because a trade publication went looking for a midsize-bank AI success story. A related claim that 81% of North American banks changed build-versus-buy strategy due to AI comes from a venture-capital-sponsored report and is excluded.

finding: AI-skill job postings carry a 28% salary premium and a majority of them now sit outside IT and computer science, while US government projections split the technical occupations - computer programmers projected to decline 7% over 2025-2035 partly due to AI, and software developers, QA analysts and testers projected to grow 10%.
evidence: Lightcast analysis of over 1.3 billion job postings, published 23 July 2025: postings requiring AI skills 'offer 28% higher salaries - nearly $18,000 more per year' | Same analysis: '51% of job postings requiring AI skills are outside IT and computer science occupations', with '800% growth in generative AI roles across non-tech industries since 2022' and about 40% growth in AI skill demand within finance roles off a low base, concentrated among quantitative analysts | BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: 'Employment of computer programmers is projected to decline 7 percent from 2025 to 2035', noting 'many companies are expected to leverage technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), to automate repetitive programming tasks' | BLS: 'Overall employment of software developers, quality assurance analysts, and testers is projected to grow 10 percent from 2025 to 2035', against 3% projected growth for all occupations
old_way: AI's effect on team shape is assumed to be an engineering-organisation question, tracked through software job markets and answered with headcount in the technology function.
new_way: The premium and the demand growth are diffusing fastest into non-technical functions, while inside technology the effect splits by how narrowly the role is defined - the narrow implementation role is projected to shrink and the broader design-and-test role to grow faster than the economy.
so_what: For org design the conclusion is not 'fewer engineers'. It is that an AI-fluency line belongs in job requisitions across marketing, risk, operations and quantitative functions, not just engineering, and that compensation bands outside technology will feel the 28% premium first. Inside technology, the planning question is whether a role is defined narrowly enough to be the one BLS expects to decline.
verification_note: All three pages fetched this run and every figure quoted appears in the fetched text. Lightcast is a commercial labour-market data vendor with a disclosed large-N method but a clear interest in demonstrating the relevance of its own dataset, so this is capped at B and never used as sole support. Job postings measure demand signals, not filled roles or actual pay. The BLS figures are government data but are ten-year forward projections, not measured historical change, and are labelled as such; BLS publishes no finance-industry breakdown for these occupations. The Lightcast finance figure is growth off an explicitly low base and should not be read as absolute scale.

finding: In a randomised controlled trial, 16 experienced open-source developers took 19% longer to complete real issues in their own repositories when allowed to use AI tools, while both before and after the trial they believed AI had made them roughly 20% faster.
evidence: 16 developers completed 246 real issues, 136 AI-allowed and 110 AI-disallowed, on repositories averaging 23,000 stars they regularly contribute to, with AI use randomly assigned per issue | Result, verbatim: 'we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%' | Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still estimated a 20% speedup afterwards; 34 economics experts and 54 machine-learning experts forecast speedups of 39% and 38% | The raw ratio of average times gives a 34% slowdown; 19% is the regression-adjusted estimate controlling for developers' pre-randomisation difficulty forecasts | Screen-recording labelling of 74 issues shows AI-allowed time shifting away from active coding toward prompting, waiting for and reviewing AI output
old_way: The default premise under nearly every AI coding claim, including vendor and internal ones, that AI assistance shortens completion time on real engineering work in familiar codebases.
new_way: On this task mix - complex changes to large codebases by their own experienced maintainers - AI access measurably lengthened completion time, and developer self-assessment moved in the opposite direction from the measured result.
so_what: Constrains every BUILD-stage claim of AI-driven engineering speedup in this research, and by extension the OPERATE rows that assume engineering capacity is being released. The specific damage is to methodology, not magnitude: a perception-reality gap this large means any 'we ship faster with AI' claim resting on developer recall or survey self-report is not evidence. Demand instrumented cycle-time or a holdout before accepting one, including from your own teams.
verification_note: Blog fetched this run and the full 51-page paper downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF; every figure above was read from the extracted text. Important limit on precision: the paper states it reports 95% confidence intervals using HC3 standard errors and that a hierarchical bootstrap 'yields somewhat wider confidence intervals', but the numeric interval around the 19% estimate appears only in Figure 1, and per the brief chart values are not quoted as text - so the 19% should be treated as a point estimate of uncertain width, not a precise quantity. Vintage caveat cutting against the finding, from the paper itself: most issues were completed in February and March 2025 using Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet, 'before models like Claude 4 Opus or Gemini 2.5 Pro were released'. N=16 is small and tasks came from participants' own repositories. Authors state their results do not show AI fails to speed up most developers and do not generalise beyond software development. METR sells no AI product, which cuts against remedy-selling bias, but a contrarian result carries its own virality incentive.

finding: The widely quoted claim that 95% of enterprise generative-AI initiatives return nothing comes from a preliminary, non-peer-reviewed MIT Project NANDA report resting on 52 interviews, 153 conference-collected survey responses and 300 public initiatives, whose headline exhibit contradicts its own prose and which rates Financial Services at 0.5 out of 5 on its own disruption index.
evidence: Report methodology note, verbatim: 'a systematic review of over 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, structured interviews with representatives from 52 organizations, and survey responses from 153 senior leaders collected across four major industry conferences', research period January to June 2025 | Executive summary: 'Despite $30-40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI... 95% of organizations are getting zero return', and separately 'Sixty percent of organizations evaluated such tools, but only 20 percent reached pilot stage and just 5 percent reached production' | Success definition, verbatim: 'Success defined as deployment beyond pilot phase with measurable KPIs. ROI impact measured 6 months post-pilot' and elsewhere as tools 'users or executives have remarked as causing a marked and sustained productivity and/or P&L impact' | Report's own limitation, verbatim: 'These figures are directionally accurate based on individual interviews rather than official company reporting. Sample sizes vary by category, and success definitions may differ across organizations' | The disruption-index exhibit scores Financial Services 0.5 out of 5 with the key signal 'Backend automation; customer relationships stable'
old_way: The 95% figure is quoted as a hard industry statistic - usually via a news article, usually without a sample size - by both sceptics dismissing AI and vendors selling the remedy for it.
new_way: Read at source it is a directional finding from a small interview base with a six-month ROI window the authors concede 'may be insufficient', an inconsistent denominator, and an organisation behind it that promotes the class of AI infrastructure it finds the market lacking.
so_what: Constrains every ANNOUNCED and PILOT maturity claim across SENSE, IDEATE, BUILD, LAUNCH, MEASURE and LEARN in this research - and constrains the finance-specific claims hardest, since this study rates Financial Services among its least-disrupted sectors with change confined to the back office. Use it to set expectations about pilot-to-production odds; do not use it as a precise failure rate, because it is not one, and anyone in the room who has read the source can dismantle it.
verification_note: The 26-page PDF was downloaded and text-extracted with PyMuPDF this run and page 5 was additionally rendered to an image and read visually to confirm chart label-to-value pairing. That visual check found a substantive error repeated in earlier drafts and in wide secondary coverage: the disruption-index chart plots only seven bars and does not plot Technology at all, with Media and Telecom at 2 and Professional Services at 1.5 - so the commonly reported 'Technology 2.0, Media and Telecom 1.5' pairing is wrong. Financial Services at 0.5 is visually confirmed, tied with Healthcare and Pharma, Consumer and Retail and Advanced Industries, above only Energy and Materials at 0. The report is also internally inconsistent on its own denominator, saying 'only 2 of 8 major sectors' in one place and 'seven of nine sectors' in another while its table lists eight. Preliminary and non-peer-reviewed by its own front matter; underlying interview and survey data not published; all company data anonymised so nothing is independently checkable. Sponsor interest disclosed: Project NANDA's research mission promotes learning-capable and agentic AI infrastructure, giving it an interest in portraying current non-agentic enterprise approaches as failing. finding: Klarna's claim that its AI assistant did the work of 700 full-time customer service agents was followed roughly fifteen months later by its CEO conceding that cost had been too dominant a factor and had produced lower quality, and by a recruitment drive to put humans back in front of customers.

finding: Linking adoption surveys of 25,000 Danish workers to government administrative earnings records, an NBER working paper estimates precise null effects of AI chatbot use on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT's launch, ruling out effects larger than 2% despite widespread employer adoption and self-reported productivity gains.

old_way: Measured or self-reported productivity gains from AI are assumed to translate within a couple of years into the hard outcomes a CFO would recognise - hours, earnings, headcount - and case studies rest on that assumption without testing it.
new_way: Widespread adoption and genuine self-reported productivity gains coexist with a precisely estimated zero effect on earnings and hours across two years; what changes first is the composition of tasks and which occupations people move into, not pay or hours.
so_what: Constrains OPERATE-stage claims about AI-driven headcount and compensation effects throughout this research, including the bank rows in this very group. finding: Two firms running industrial-scale online experimentation report, from their own platform data, that only a minority of well-designed experiments improve the metric they were built to improve: about one-third at Microsoft in 2009 and about 12 percent at Spotify in 2025.

old_way: Experimentation programmes are judged on win rate, the share of tests that ship a positive change, so a programme where most tests fail looks broken, creating pressure to stop testing, re-run until something wins, or ship on judgement instead.
new_way: Both firms publish the base rate rather than hiding it, and Spotify replaces win rate with learning rate as the programme's headline metric, counting a detected regression or an adequately powered null result as a successful experiment.
so_what: The base rate of success for a well-designed product idea is roughly 1-in-3 at best and closer to 1-in-8 at a modern consumer-scale firm, measured by the firms themselves sixteen years apart. Any investment case for measurement therefore rests on testing throughput and honesty of the read, not on picking winners up front; and the correct KPI for a measurement function is the share of decisions it makes trustworthy, not the share it makes positive.

finding: Microsoft's CUPED variance-reduction technique, running live in Bing's experimentation system, cut key-metric variance by about 50 percent, letting an experiment reach the same statistical power with about half the users or half the duration.
evidence: Abstract, verbatim: "The results on Bing's experimentation system are very successful: we can reduce variance by about 50%, effectively achieving the same statistical power with only half of the users, or half the duration" | Conclusion reports three specific live cases, verbatim: "Three important recent experiments showed variance reductions of 45%, 52% and 49% with one week of experiment and one week of pre-experiment data" | Paper states "CUPED is currently live in Bing's online experimentation system" | Method regresses the outcome metric on a pre-experiment covariate, most often the same metric measured before the experiment began
old_way: Required sample size and run length are fixed by the raw variance of the outcome metric, so detecting effects on the order of fractions of a percent forces either very large samples or long runtimes, and experimentation gets rationed to the few decisions judged to deserve it.
new_way: Pre-experiment behavioural data is used as a covariate to strip out variance unrelated to the treatment, roughly halving the users or the time needed to detect the same effect, so many more decisions fit inside the same traffic and calendar.
so_what: This is the specific lever that makes always-on experimentation affordable, and it answers the objection that testing every decision is too slow and too costly with a peer-reviewed number rather than an assertion. It also sets the honest baseline for AI-era experimentation vendors: the roughly 2x sensitivity gain their platforms are built on is a 2013 regression adjustment, not a model, so a vendor claiming AI delivers it is reselling statistics.

finding: A sequential anytime-valid testing method developed by Netflix researchers with a Harvard Business School co-author, published in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, lets A/B tests be monitored continuously and stopped early with formal Type-I error control, removing the statistical penalty for peeking.
evidence: Paper "Anytime-Valid Linear Models and Regression Adjusted Causal Inference in Randomized Experiments", Lindon, Ham, Tingley (Netflix) and Bojinov | Abstract, verbatim: the method "formally allows experiments to be continuously monitored for significance, stopped early, and safeguards against statistical malpractices in data collection" | Validated on production data rather than simulation alone, verbatim: "We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach through simulations and applications to real A/B test data from Netflix" | arXiv record carries journal DOI 10.1080/01621459.2026.2692052 (JASA); first submitted October 2022, v5 revised 7 July 2025
old_way: Fixed-horizon t-tests and F-tests are valid only if the sample size is committed in advance, so checking results early and stopping at first significance inflates the false-positive rate; teams must wait out a pre-set duration or accept a read they cannot defend.
new_way: Confidence sequences that remain valid at every sample size let an experiment be watched continuously and stopped the moment an effect is established, or killed early to halt a harmful release, with the error guarantee intact.
so_what: This defuses the objection that faster reads must mean sloppier reads: it is a formal guarantee, not a tradeoff. It is also the precondition for any continuously-monitored or agent-surfaced experiment dashboard being statistically legitimate rather than an industrialised peeking machine, so it should gate procurement of always-on analytics tooling: ask the vendor which sequential method underlies the live significance indicator.
