finding: In a research prototype, 1,000 persona-conditioned LLM agents shopping on a live Amazon.com interface produced a statistically significant difference between two product-filter designs, demonstrating LLM agents acting as the experimental subjects rather than as the thing being tested.

old_way: A directional read on a UX or product-design change requires either exposing real customer traffic to a variant that carries live business risk while it runs, or commissioning a slow and costly human usability study first.
new_way: Populate the test with simulated agent subjects to get a directional behavioural read on a staged or live interface before any real customer is exposed to the risky variant.
so_what: This is the one place in the measurement stage where AI is the instrument rather than the subject, and it is worth a roadmap slot as a pre-screen that narrows which variants earn live traffic. finding: The CFPB's April 2026 Regulation B final rule removed the effects test from ECOA's implementing regulation and official commentary and replaced disparate-impact exposure with an intent-based standard, narrowing the fair-lending objection to randomised testing of credit offer terms.
evidence: CFPB eRegulations text of 12 CFR 1002.6(a) official interpretation, verbatim: "The Act does not provide that the 'effects test' applies for determining whether there is discrimination in violation of the Act" | Same interpretation, verbatim: "The Act does not provide for the prohibition of practices that are facially neutral as to prohibited bases, except to the extent that facially neutral criteria function as proxies for protected characteristics designed or applied with the intention of advantaging or disadvantaging individuals based on protected characteristics" | CFPB final-rule page states the rule "amends provisions related to disparate impact, discouragement of applicants or prospective applicants, and special purpose credit programs under Regulation B", issued 22 April 2026, effective 21 July 2026
old_way: A facially neutral practice, including a randomised test of credit terms that produced statistically different outcomes across a protected class with no intent behind it, could itself support an ECOA disparate-impact claim. This is the standard reason legal and compliance functions block randomisation of price, credit line and approval thresholds.
new_way: Federal ECOA liability turns on intentional differential treatment, including intentionally applied proxies; a statistical outcome disparity alone no longer establishes the violation, which narrows without eliminating the exposure created by randomised offer-term testing.
so_what: The single most common blocker this audience raises against experimentation in credit - fair lending law means we cannot A/B test - is materially weaker as a blanket federal claim than it was six months ago. The correct ask is a re-scoped legal opinion on what may now be randomised, not an open field: intentionally proxy-based targeting is still prohibited, state fair-lending statutes and UDAAP exposure are untouched, and the rule is months old and untested by examiners or courts. Governance is the adjacent stage; the change here is to what a lender is permitted to measure.

finding: The UK FCA's regulatory sandbox is a supervised live-testing mechanism in which firms run real transactions with real consumers under bespoke safeguards and a mandatory exit plan, and the FCA's own evaluation of its first two cohorts shows it produced both commercial signal and a kill switch that actually fired.

finding: Credit underwriting models cannot be validated until 12 to 24 months of loan performance have accumulated, because standard practice is to wait until 70 to 90 percent of a vintage's eventual default events have emerged before the outcome data is treated as usable.
evidence: FinRegLab methodological appendix, verbatim: "With regard to choosing a performance window, model developers typically use between 12 months and 24 months" | Verbatim: "in practice most model developers aim for a performance period in which 70% to 90% of default events have emerged for a particular product" | The appendix names three drivers of the window - completeness of default emergence, representativeness of the development sample as the economy drifts, and time decay of predictive power, since "A longer performance window therefore introduces additional noise to the target variable" | The study itself chose 12 months "because it allowed us to avoid the risk that COVID-19 impacted the performance data and because it is generally consistent with industry practice"
old_way: The tech-style test-and-learn cadence of shipping a variant and reading a result in days or weeks is structurally unavailable in credit, and inside firms the resulting wait is often explained away as regulatory caution or institutional conservatism.
new_way: The window is named as a deliberate statistical compromise with three stated drivers, so any change to underwriting criteria carries a de facto minimum observation period of 12 to 24 months before its true risk impact is knowable, however fast the approval-rate read comes back.
so_what: This is the honest constraint on any claim that AI makes measurement fast in lending, and it is the one to concede before the room raises it: the binding delay is the arrival rate of defaults, not model training time or analyst capacity, so no AI tool shortens it by itself. It also gives a precise test for any proposal claiming to compress the credit feedback loop - show that it changes the outcome variable to an earlier-observable proxy validated against the eventual 12-to-24-month outcome, rather than merely speeding up the analysis of the same lagging one.

finding: In FinRegLab's controlled comparison on a combined credit-bureau and bank-transaction dataset, machine learning improved predictive accuracy by up to 2 percent over logistic regression built on the same data and raised simulated approval rates by as much as 4 percent at mainstream risk cutoffs, without raising default risk.
evidence: Verbatim: "Machine learning models improved predictive accuracy by up to 2% compared to logistic regression models built with the same data, which increased credit approval rates by as much as 4% in simulations with risk thresholds likely to be used by mainstream lenders" | Scale translation in the same factsheet: against roughly "55 million new credit card accounts and 3.8 million new mortgages" originated in 2023 at similar cutoffs, a 4 percent increase works out to "roughly two million additional credit card accounts and 152,000 additional mortgages" | The ML model combining bureau and cash-flow data "had the highest predictive accuracy and generally had the highest approval rates at various cut offs", while the bureau-only ML model "frequently ranked second on both metrics" | Approval-rate gains were "particularly large and consistent across models for consumers with recent derogatory history", and reductions in approvals of consumers who went on to default were largest for low-to-moderate income populations
old_way: Underwriting approaches are compared using traditional logistic regression on credit-bureau data inside the same fixed 12-to-24-month performance window, and the accuracy of that read is treated as roughly fixed once the data source is fixed.
new_way: Within an unchanged observation window, machine learning and cash-flow data extract measurably more signal about the same eventual outcome, framed by the researchers as expanding access at a constant risk tolerance rather than as shortening the window.
so_what: This is the defensible version of the AI-in-credit claim and it is deliberately unexciting: AI did not compress time-to-signal at all, because the 12-month window was held constant - it extracted more usable signal from the same window. Paired with MEASURE-08 the argument to leadership becomes precise and much harder to dismiss: fund better inference inside the existing loop, and stop promising a faster one. The distributional detail is the commercial hook - the largest approval gains fell on consumers with recent derogatory history, a population current scorecards systematically misprice.
verification_note: Factsheet PDF downloaded and extracted with PyMuPDF in this run; every quoted figure above is verbatim in the extracted text. CORRECTION: the source slice rendered the headline as up to 2 percentage points of AUC-type accuracy. The factsheet says only up to 2 percent, does not state whether this is percentage points or a relative change, and does not name the metric; the companion appendix, also fetched here, states the primary performance metric was ROC-AUC but never restates the 2 percent figure, so the percentage-points-of-AUC gloss was unsupported and has been removed. The slice's second URL, the finreglab.org research landing page, was NOT fetched in this run and has been dropped per the brief's fetched-only rule; the appendix PDF, which was fetched, replaces it. The up-to and as-much-as framing is the source's own (brief trap 4) and is retained because it is anchored to a stated comparison and translated into absolute origination volumes rather than left as a bare marketing range. This is a simulation on a single anonymised bureau-plus-aggregator dataset, originations April 2018 to March 2019 with 12 months of performance - maturity RESEARCH, not a live deployment - and the appendix discloses that the validation sample is near-contemporaneous with the development sample rather than out-of-time. FinRegLab funders not confirmed in this run.

finding: The MIT NANDA report's own stated core barrier to scaling enterprise generative AI is not model quality, infrastructure, regulation or talent but learning: deployed tools that do not retain feedback, adapt to context or improve with use.
evidence: Verbatim: "The core barrier to scaling is not infrastructure, regulation, or talent. It is learning. Most GenAI systems do not retain feedback, adapt to context, or improve over time" | Enterprise tool funnel, verbatim: "Sixty percent of organizations evaluated such tools, but only 20 percent reached pilot stage and just 5 percent reached production" | Section 4.3 takeaway, verbatim: "For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. The gap is structural, GenAI lacks memory and adaptability" | Stated method: "a systematic review of over 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, structured interviews with representatives from 52 organizations, and survey responses from 153 senior leaders collected across four major industry conferences", research period January to June 2025
old_way: A pilot is judged to have worked if it produced a good demo or a one-off report; the underlying tool is stateless, re-answers the same question the same way every time, and nothing a completed pilot established changes how the next one is built.
new_way: Persistence is reframed as the property that separates tools reaching production from tools that stall - systems that retain context, ingest outcome feedback and visibly improve - making the learning stage an architectural requirement rather than a reporting afterthought.
so_what: If this is even directionally right, the stalled-pilot problem is not fixed by a better foundation model, and the budget line that matters is state, feedback capture and retraining pipelines rather than model licences. Hold the claim at exactly that level in front of this audience: this report is the origin of the widely-mangled 95 percent figure, so leading with the mechanism and explicitly disowning the headline is what keeps the row from becoming the weak link someone uses to dismiss the set.
verification_note: Brief domain trap 1. The full PDF was downloaded and extracted with PyMuPDF in this run rather than read through a news write-up, and every passage quoted above is verbatim. PRECISION ON THE HEADLINE: the report's actual claim is that 95 percent of organizations are getting zero return on 30 to 40 billion dollars of enterprise GenAI investment, and elsewhere the 95 percent failure rate for enterprise AI solutions - it is NOT 95 percent of AI pilots fail, which is the form it is almost always quoted in. CORRECTIONS to the source slice: (a) the slice called the learning gap the leading cause, but the report's own barrier survey ranks resistance to adopting new tools FIRST and the learning gap second, with learning elevated to core barrier only in the authors' framing, so leading cause overstated their own chart and has been softened; (b) the slice attributed the 90 percent prefer-humans figure to tools lacking memory across sessions, but the 90 percent measures preference for humans on complex multi-week projects and the memory explanation is the authors' interpretation rather than what the number measures, and the underlying 90 percent is chart-embedded with only the takeaway sentence in body text. DOWNGRADED from the slice's B to C: self-reported interview and survey data with no filed or audited component; the 153-respondent survey is a convenience sample recruited across four industry conferences; the report labels itself Preliminary Findings; all company data is anonymised; and its own research note concedes barrier scores reflect reported frequency rather than objective measurement. Sponsor interest is live and must be disclosed whenever this is shown - Project NANDA promotes agent-based AI infrastructure, so systems need memory and agency is simultaneously its finding and its thesis. The slice's second URL, a personal blog at jorgep.com, was dropped as below the evidence bar. Per the compile brief this row is scoped to the organisational-learning angle only; the failure-rate angle belongs to the COUNTER group and is deliberately not argued here.

finding: On three public credit datasets, a scoring model retrained only on the outcomes of applicants it previously approved - the standard closed loop in production underwriting - posted higher measured accuracy than a model given true labels for every applicant, so rising accuracy on the approved book is not evidence the loop is healthy.
evidence: Paper "The Illusion of Improvement: Reject Inference Strategies in Credit Scoring" by Bruno Scarone (Northeastern University) and Ricardo Baeza-Yates (KTH Royal Institute of Technology) | The biased approved-only model scored "accuracy of 0.833 versus 0.816 on Default/GBDT at t=10" against an oracle model holding true labels for all applicants, despite having strictly less information | A standard remedy, extrapolating labels for rejected applicants, moved the training-set default rate "from 22.1% to 26.8%" against a true population rate of 22.1 percent, relocating the bias rather than removing it | Datasets: Default (30,000 records), PPDai (31,230 after dropping missing values), LendingClub (279,520 after preprocessing); the authors report that "even minimal exploration rates (2%-5%)" surface the hidden bias
old_way: The underwriting model is retrained on the bank's own book of approved loans, so the feedback loop only ever contains outcomes for applicants the model already said yes to, and improving accuracy on that closed population is read as the model getting better.
new_way: That improvement is shown to be partly an artefact, since a biased model can beat a fully-informed one on standard accuracy, and small deliberate exploration - approving a slice of marginal rejects specifically to generate feedback - is demonstrated as a cheap way to detect the drift before it compounds.
so_what: An automated feedback loop in a live underwriting or credit-line model can get quietly worse at exactly the population it never approves, which is a fair-lending exposure, while the dashboard the model owner watches shows accuracy rising. The governance consequence is concrete and actionable: portfolio-level accuracy is not a valid health check for a closed-loop credit model, and monitoring needs a funded exploration budget - which nobody approves by default, because it books as deliberately accepted losses rather than as measurement spend.
verification_note: arXiv HTML v3 (18 September 2026) fetched in this run; the 0.833 against 0.816 comparison, the 22.1 to 26.8 percent shift and all three dataset record counts are present in the fetched text. CORRECTION: the source slice stated that 2-to-5-percent exploration revealed the bias at a measured accuracy cost of under 0.5 percent. That figure does not appear in the paper; the stated cost is approximately 1.5 percent accuracy at FULL exploration (r=1.0), so the under-0.5-percent claim has been REMOVED and replaced with the paper's own wording about minimal exploration rates. source_type corrected from the slice's PEER_REVIEWED to RESEARCH_FIRM: this is an unrefereed arXiv preprint with no confirmed publication venue, which the slice's own note conceded while still filing it as peer-reviewed. Held at B rather than C because the method is disclosed, the three datasets are public and named, and the result is reproducible in principle. Crucially this is a simulation study on public datasets and NOT a disclosed failure from any named bank's live loop - it demonstrates the mechanism convincingly, it does not document an occurrence, and it should never be presented as one.

finding: Zillow's algorithmic home-buying programme booked a 304 million dollar inventory write-down and was shut down entirely in Q3 2021 because the read on forecast-versus-actual price error existed as a quarterly reporting metric rather than as a control on purchasing, so the company kept buying at the old model's prices for a full quarter after the market turned.
evidence: Q3 2021 shareholder letter, filed as Exhibit 99.3 to an SEC Form 8-K, verbatim: a "$304 million write-down on inventory owned at the end of Q3" | Zillow Offers unit economics swung "approximately 1,200 basis points from Q2 to an expected -500 to -700 basis points in Q4 2021" | The company purchased 9,680 homes while selling only 3,032 in the same quarter | The wind-down included a "reduction in our workforce of approximately 25% over the next few quarters"
old_way: A pricing model's output is trusted as the decision itself - buy at the algorithm's price, in volume, continuously - while reconciliation of predicted against actual resale price is treated as lagging financial reporting reviewed on a quarterly cycle.
new_way: After the fact the same signal, the forecast-versus-actual price gap, became the reason to halt an entire product line; the read had existed throughout, but it only became a decision once the loss was already booked.
so_what: This is the price of a loop that reports but does not decide, quantified in a filed document: 304 million dollars and a quarter of the workforce. The diagnostic it hands a stakeholder is not do we measure this but what is the shortest path from this metric moving to someone being required to stop - and if that path runs through a quarterly review, the loop is open no matter how good the model is, because the buying continues while the evidence accumulates. Ask it of every algorithmic pricing, credit-line and limit-assignment loop in the book.
verification_note: SEC-filed shareholder letter fetched in this run; all four figures above are verbatim in the fetched text. REFINEMENT on the source slice: the approximately 1,200 basis point swing runs from Q2 to an EXPECTED minus 500 to minus 700 basis points in Q4 2021, so it is partly a forward-looking estimate rather than a fully realised move, and the slice cited it without that qualifier. The slice's two additional quotations - much more than we modeled as possible, and a safe business to be in - were not re-confirmed in this pass and have been DROPPED from evidence rather than carried forward unverified. Vintage caveat, material: this is a 2021 pre-LLM statistical and ML pricing model, filed PREDICTIVE, and it is evidence about decision-loop latency, not about any current-frontier AI capability - do not present it as the latter. Cross-industry rather than finserv; included because the mechanism transfers directly to any algorithmic price or line-assignment loop. The corroborating academic paper the source slice mentioned, Malik and Manzoor arXiv 2302.09438, was not fetched in this run and is deliberately not cited.

finding: Upstart's personal-loan underwriting model is a continuously retrained closed loop trained on an expanding base of actual repayment outcomes rather than a fixed development sample, and the company files the resulting full-automation rate as a rising year-on-year metric.
evidence: FY2025 Form 10-K: the personal loan model "expanded from 23 variables at the end of 2014 to over 2,500 [variables] at the end of 2025" and "as of December 31, 2025, this model was trained on nearly 104 million repayment events" | It is one of "approximately 30 proprietary machine learning models that we developed in-house" | "In the year ended December 31, 2025, 91% of Upstart-powered loans were fully automated, compared to approximately 70% at the time of our initial public offering in December 2020" | "Our AI models have been continuously upgraded, trained and refined for more than ten years" and "We believe the flywheel effects generated by our constantly improving AI models provide a significant competitive advantage"
old_way: A traditional scorecard is built once on a fixed historical dataset, validated, deployed, and then redeveloped only periodically - often years apart - through a discrete model-risk-management project with its own funding cycle.
new_way: The training set is defined as all repayment events to date and grows every day loans are serviced; the retraining cadence and the resulting automation rate are filed as the product's core competitive claim rather than described as a general capability.
so_what: This is the rare filed, quantified instance of production outcomes flowing automatically back into the model that makes the next decision, inside a regulated US consumer-lending product - so the closed loop is demonstrably buildable under fair-lending supervision, and the benchmark for a bank's own underwriting loop is now a named competitor's disclosed numbers rather than an abstraction. Read it directly against LEARN-02: 104 million repayment events are 104 million outcomes from applicants Upstart approved, so the scale and speed of the loop do nothing by themselves about the reject-inference blind spot, and the company presents that scale as a moat.
verification_note: Filed Form 10-K for FY2025 on SEC EDGAR, fetched in this run; every figure quoted above is present and explicitly stated in the filing. These are the company's own operational metrics about its own product - narrative business-section disclosure, not GAAP-audited financial statement data, and not independently verified by any regulator within this document - carrying obvious self-interest and survivorship framing, since a struggling continuous-learning loop would never be headlined as a flywheel. evidence_strength A reflects that this is a filed document carrying legal liability for accuracy, NOT that the operational claims were externally audited; that distinction should be stated if challenged. The source slice's reference to an independent Relman Colfax fair-lending monitorship was not re-fetched in this run and is deliberately not cited here as corroboration.

finding: Two 2026 benchmark studies of LLM-simulated survey RESPONDENTS (not AI-generated concepts) find that digital twins fail at the individual level: they do not beat a plain demographic-lookup baseline at predicting a person's attitudes, they are systematically less variable than the humans they model, and they amplify weak demographic-attitude correlations into strong ones.
evidence: Chen, Zhu & Zheng benchmark against the General Social Survey (14,704 respondents, 85,898 respondent-question pairs, 2016-2024 waves) and World Values Survey (91,774 respondents, 63 countries): on WVS every model tested is 11-22 percentage points LESS accurate than a demographic-lookup baseline | On the GSS confidence-in-banks question, a person's politics explains about 1.5% of the variation in real answers, yet the models behave as though it explains up to roughly 67% - the paper calls this an approximately 45-fold exaggeration - and the models' top-scoring segment differs from the true human top segment for 50% of GSS and 72% of WVS question-axis pairs | Peng et al. (23 authors, Columbia/Yale, 19 pre-registered studies, 164 outcomes): twin response standard deviation is lower than human standard deviation in 154 of 164 cases (93.9%) | In the same mega-study, average individual-level point accuracy is 0.748 but the average twin-to-human rank-order correlation is only 0.197, and accuracy is systematically higher for higher-education, higher-income and moderate-politics participants
old_way: Segment attitude and confidence reads produced by fielding probability-sample surveys, where demographic-attitude correlations are measured rather than assumed, and subgroup accuracy is empirically testable.
new_way: LLM personas or 'digital twins' conditioned on demographics or on a person's prior survey answers, queried repeatedly as a cheap standing panel.
so_what: The failure is not a tolerable accuracy haircut - it is directional. A synthetic panel would have told a bank that trust-in-banks is mostly a political-identity story when in the real data politics explains about one part in seventy, and it picks the wrong priority segment in half to three-quarters of questions. Worse for a finserv research function: twins are most accurate for the affluent, educated respondents whose behaviour you already understand, and least accurate for the mass-market and lower-income segments that drive inclusion, fair-lending and growth questions. Any IDEATE-stage sizing built on this signal inherits a mis-targeted segment before a single concept is written.
verification_note: MERGED from two separate slice findings that made the same core claim from different datasets; union of evidence retained. Every figure above was re-fetched and located in the HTML text in this run. Both papers are preprints, NOT confirmed peer-reviewed: Chen et al. state 'This manuscript is currently under peer review'; Peng et al. is arXiv:2509.19088v5 (19 Apr 2026) building on the peer-reviewed Twin-2K-500 database. source_type therefore recorded as RESEARCH_FIRM rather than PEER_REVIEWED, and strength capped at B. CORRECTION: the source slice said politics was inflated 'roughly 40-fold'; the paper's own wording is 'approximately a 45-fold exaggeration' and it hedges the 67% as 'up to roughly 67%' - both corrected here. Neither paper is finance-specific: the bank-confidence item is one GSS question, so industry is coded CROSS_INDUSTRY rather than BANKING to avoid overstating finserv relevance. No commercial synthetic-panel vendor is involved in either study; academic authors only. source_date is the later of the two papers (Chen et al., 2026-07); Peng et al. is 2026-04.

finding: A refereed operational-risk method shows that the CFPB's free, public consumer-complaint narratives can be machine-read at corpus scale to flag systematic patterns of non-meritorious complaints, a detection task the authors state both classification algorithms and human reviewers fail at when working alone.
evidence: Gao, Sun, Wang, Yang & Zitikis, 'NLP-based detection of systematic anomalies among the narratives of consumer complaints', arXiv:2308.11138v3, stated on the title page as 'To appear in Journal of Operational Risk' | Illustrative corpus: CFPB Consumer Complaint Database credit-card and prepaid-card complaints against one unnamed major bank, submitted 1 Dec 2011 to 29 Jun 2023, narrowed to 2,905 records and finally 2,849 complaints, of which 1,051 were meritorious (resolved with some relief) | Five classifiers were compared (logistic regression, SVM, gradient boosting, MLP, random forest), each trained on a random 60/40 split repeated 500 times; the Support Vector Machine outperformed the others | The paper's stated motivation is that for 'smaller and frequent systematic patterns of non-meritorious complaints' classification algorithms 'may falter', and that bulk complaint datasets exist partly because using complaints for regulatory purposes is 'significantly more cost-effective than resolving them individually'
old_way: Complaint narratives triaged case by case inside the firm and inside the regulator, so cross-complaint patterns - templated filings, a servicing defect generating a recognisable narrative shape - are visible only to whoever happens to read enough of them.
new_way: Classification plus a statistical anomaly index run across the whole public complaint corpus, surfacing clusters that share a systematic pattern rather than adjudicating each complaint.
so_what: The asymmetry, not the method, is the point. This corpus is free and open, so a competitor, a plaintiff firm, a short seller or a journalist can now run pattern-level early warning on your product and servicing lines before your own complaint-ops function has closed the quarter. If your SENSE stage treats complaints as a compliance record to be resolved rather than a signal to be mined, someone outside the bank is reading your book before you are.
verification_note: WebFetch cannot parse the arXiv PDF stream; downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF in this run. All figures above located in the extracted text (the paper formats numbers with thin spaces, e.g. '2 905', which is why a naive comma search misses them). The acknowledgements thank 'two anonymous referees', so the work has been refereed, but the title page says 'To appear', i.e. accepted and not yet in print - final journal issue could not be confirmed, so strength is capped at B. The bank is deliberately unnamed by the authors; company is N/A and no claim is made about that bank's own outcomes, only about the method. Authors are academic and insurance-industry affiliated (Western University, Dalhousie, Canada Life, Icahn School of Medicine); none are CFPB-affiliated, so this is NOT evidence of the CFPB's own operational practice. Classical NLP/ML, not an LLM - filed PREDICTIVE.

company: MULTIPLE (LISCC banks plus large, regional and community banking organisations; about 100 banks per quarter)
finding: Federal Reserve Bank researchers ran locally-hosted open-source LLMs over about 100 US banks' quarterly earnings-call transcripts and showed that both the share of remarks devoted to deposits and the cross-bank similarity of topics discussed hit their sample peak in the same quarter as the SVB, Signature and First Republic failures.
evidence: Cook, Kazinnik, Lundgaard Hansen & McAdam, 'Evaluating Local Language Models: An Application to Financial Earnings Calls', Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Research Working Paper RWP 23-12, November 2023, doi 10.18651/RWP2023-12 | Sample is about 100 banks per quarter, 2021 through 2023Q2, with transcripts split into a corpus of about 120 thousand individual speaker passages, roughly 12 thousand per quarter | Deposits are the topic of less than 1% of a bank's remarks in the low-stress episode (2021 Q2-Q3), and the frequency of deposit discussion 'jumps by over 200%, to a peak' during the 2023Q1 high-stress episode | Mean pairwise cosine similarity of 150-element topic vectors across the bank cross-section is stated in the text to jump 'to its peak in the first quarter of 2023' and to descend 'to a nadir in q2 and q3 of 2021' | Models are open-weight and run locally (Vicuna 7B/13B, Guanaco 33B/65B, Fin-LLaMA 33B, Wizard-Vicuna 30B), most 4-bit quantised, chosen so confidential text never leaves the premises
old_way: Competitive-intelligence and risk desks read transcripts one bank at a time, or dictionary-score them with fixed word lists; thematic convergence across the sector around an emerging risk is recognised in hindsight, after individual banks have separately disclosed it.
new_way: Open-weight LLMs running on the firm's own hardware label topic, sentiment, clarity and temporal orientation for every passage of every bank's call, so a cross-sectional convergence measure exists for the whole sector in the quarter the event happens.
so_what: The signal that would have flagged sector-wide deposit-flight anxiety was sitting in public transcripts you already receive, and reading them the old way could not surface it because the signal is cross-sectional - it lives in how similar every bank suddenly sounds, not in what any one bank says. A desk still doing periodic manual review is structurally incapable of computing it. And the deployment answer to the usual objection is in the paper: these are open-weight models on local hardware, so 'we cannot send confidential text to a cloud API' is no longer a reason not to have this.
verification_note: kansascityfed.org hung on repeated curl attempts in this run; the PDF was finally retrieved via WebFetch and the resulting 53-page binary text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF. The >200% deposits jump, the under-1% baseline, the ~100 banks/quarter, the ~120k/~12k passage counts and the 2023Q1 similarity peak / 2021 Q2-Q3 nadir are all confirmed as prose in the extracted text, not read off a chart. CORRECTION: the source slice attributed specific scoring tasks to specific models ('Vicuna 13B for sentiment, Vicuna 7B for clarity/topics, Guanaco 65B for temporal orientation'); that mapping could not be located in the extracted text and has been removed, replaced with the verified model roster. This is a research demonstration by Fed staff, NOT a deployed supervisory tool - filed RESEARCH, not PRODUCTION. The paper carries the standard disclaimer that views are the authors' and not the Federal Reserve's. Survivorship caveat: this is a result the Fed chose to publish, not an independent audit of the method's reliability.

finding: From 2019 ESMA combined web scraping with NLP to read and compare more than 20,000 retail investment product disclosure documents across the EU, and its own account in an FSB report states the exercise enabled comparison of document information 'that was previously impossible to compare'.
evidence: Financial Stability Board, 'The Use of Supervisory and Regulatory Technology by Authorities and Regulated Institutions', October 2020, Annex 1 Case Study 7 (ESMA) | Scope: more than 20,000 Key Information Documents filed under the EU PRIIPs Regulation, from more than 500 issuers, in 21 EU languages, retrieved by web scraping of external sources plus ESMA's internal databases | Findings: certain PRIIPs provisions 'were being misapplied to such an extent that suggests some confusion on how the provisions are set out', and the percentage compliance with inserting the more than 50 required words and phrases into a KID 'varies substantially across language groups' | A third finding on the investment-return simulation scenarios is described in the source as supporting the then-current ESMA and European Supervisory Authorities consultation on revising the PRIIPs KID rules | A second authority, Italy's CONSOB, appears separately in the same report (Case Study 14) pursuing deep-learning NLP for market surveillance, though its outcomes are described as expected rather than realised
old_way: Product-disclosure supervision by manual spot-check of individual documents, because checking tens of thousands of multi-language filings by hand 'cannot be performed systematically' in the report's own words.
new_way: Scrape the full population of filed disclosure documents, extract required phrases and numeric content with NLP, and compare every issuer against every other across all languages at once.
so_what: Two things change for anyone who assumes disclosure filings are effectively unread. First, the supervisor now reads the entire market's product terms simultaneously and can see that your compliance rate differs from your peers' - the spot-check era's safety margin is gone. Second, the identical capability pointed at competitors' filed rate, fee and product terms is a working automated teardown of a whole market's product book, and a regulator has already demonstrated it end to end. This is not a roadmap item; it ran from 2019.
verification_note: 76-page PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF in this run; the 20,000 KIDs, 500+ issuers, 21 EU languages, 'more than 50 required words and phrases', the 'varies substantially across language groups' line and the 'previously impossible to compare' quote are all confirmed verbatim. CORRECTION of wording from the source slice: the report does not say the 50-plus required phrases were 'misapplied'; it says certain PRIIPs provisions were misapplied AND, separately, that compliance with inserting the 50-plus required phrases varies across language groups. Jurisdiction is EU, not US - do not present this as a US supervisory practice. Vintage caveat: this documents 2019-2020 work described in a 2020 report and uses pre-LLM NLP; it is evidence that population-scale document comparison works, not evidence of current frontier capability. Rated PILOT not ANNOUNCED because the source reports realised insights; CONSOB is cited only as corroboration that a second authority pursued the same approach, since its own outcomes are stated as expected.

finding: Mechanically diffing the wording of US companies' 10-K and 10-Q filings against the prior year - detecting only that the text changed and where, with no understanding of the content - identifies firms whose future earnings, profitability and bankruptcy risk are predictable, and the market shows no abnormal price reaction on the filing date itself.
evidence: Cohen, Malloy & Nguyen, 'Lazy Prices', NBER Working Paper 25084, September 2018 (revised March 2019) | Sample covers the near-complete history of regular quarterly and annual filings by US public firms, 1995-2014 | The paper states that a portfolio shorting 'changers' and buying 'non-changers' earns 'up to 188 basis points in monthly alphas (over 22% per year) in the future' | Changes concentrated in management discussion and in the language around litigation and risk factors predict future returns, earnings, profitability, future news announcements and firm-level bankruptcies, while no abnormal price reaction occurs at the filing date, indicating the market does not read the change when it becomes public
old_way: Analysts and competitive-intelligence teams read the current filing on its own terms. Nobody line-by-line diffs this year's risk-factor or litigation language against last year's across thousands of filers, because at scale that is not a human task.
new_way: A standing automated text-difference pass over the full filing history turns 'what changed, and where' into a computable market-wide signal available every filing season.
so_what: This is the cheapest possible SENSE capability - no model, no vendor, no proprietary data, just string comparison on documents that are already free and public - and it sat unexploited long enough to leave measurable value on the table for two decades. Before funding an ambitious AI sensing programme, ask whether your competitive-intelligence function diffs competitors' filed rate sheets, fee schedules and terms of service year over year. Most do not. The capability gap at your own firm is probably not at the frontier.
verification_note: NBER page re-fetched in this run; the 'up to 188 basis points in monthly alphas (over 22% per year)' phrasing and the 1995-2014 sample are confirmed in the fetched text. CORRECTION: the source slice's so_what asserted '22%/yr' as a realised figure; the paper hedges it as 'up to', which is exactly the construction this project's brief warns about, so the hedge is carried through here and the so_what has been rewritten not to lead on the return number. NBER working papers are explicitly not peer-reviewed, so strength is capped at B; search results indicate a later Journal of Finance version but that was not fetched in this run and no peer-review status is claimed. Method is classical text similarity, not an LLM - filed PREDICTIVE per the brief's rule on pre-2023 analytics. Applies to all US filers, so CROSS_INDUSTRY; bank and insurer 10-Ks are inside the same universe. Vintage caveat: 2018 paper on 1995-2014 data.

company: MULTIPLE (Barclays, Credit Suisse, Lloyds, Nationwide, Natwest, Santander in the Phase 1 pilot, joined by HSBC across the two phases; cost survey covers large UK mortgage lenders representing about 60% of the market)
finding: The FCA and Bank of England's Digital Regulatory Reporting pilot put a number on what manual regulatory-change translation costs large UK mortgage lenders - about GBP 700k a year each in change costs alone - and then recorded that it had insufficient resources to test the NLP option for generating machine-executable code from regulatory text, leaving hand-translation as the operating method.
evidence: FCA/Bank of England Digital Regulatory Reporting, Phase 1 Report and Phase 2 Viability Assessment (published January 2020), plus the FCA's DRR programme page | Survey data estimate that large retail firms collectively accounting for 60% of the UK mortgage market spend an annual average of GBP 450k on meeting ongoing mortgage reporting obligations and a further GBP 700k on responding to new obligations and requests for additional mortgage data, with two-thirds of that being data preparation and report production | Comparing domain and total surveys, mortgage reporting alone accounted for around 5-10% of these firms' total regulatory-reporting costs | Of the routes considered for turning natural-language regulation into executable code, the Phase 1 report records for the NLP route that 'The team had insufficient resources to explore this approach during this phase of the pilot', adding only that 'some firms currently use these technologies to extract key terms from legal documents' - unnamed and unquantified
old_way: Each firm's compliance and reporting team reads published regulatory text spread across multiple documents from multiple regulators and hand-translates it into its own systems' code every time a rule changes.
new_way: A shared machine-executable version of the regulation that firms' systems consume directly, ideally generated from the regulator's own published text - which as of this pilot had not been built or tested.
so_what: Use this as the reality check on any vendor claiming AI already reads and codifies regulatory change for you. The regulators quantified the pain themselves, identified NLP-to-code as the obvious fix, and then did not attempt it. Two consequences for a SENSE-stage roadmap: the cost of regulatory horizon-scanning is real and now has a public per-firm number you can benchmark against, and the automated fix is materially less mature than the market claims - if a supplier says otherwise, ask them for the regulator-grade evidence the FCA could not produce.

finding: A sentence-level text-classification pipeline over global earnings-call transcripts decomposes each firm's risk discussion into shares attributable to specific named shocks, producing a comparable firm-level exposure series that refreshes every quarter instead of requiring a commissioned study.
evidence: Hassan, Hollander, Kalyani, van Lent, Schwedeler & Tahoun, 'Economic Surveillance using Corporate Text', NBER Working Paper 33158, November 2024 | Brexit-related sentences contributed 1.43 percent of overall risk discussion among listed firms globally in 2016Q3 (0.098 of an average 6.85 risk sentences per call) | Trade-policy risk peaked at about 0.98 percent of risk mentions in 2018Q3, comparable to Brexit's share | Covid-19 accounted for 9.88 percent of all risk sentences in 2020Q2 | The paper describes this cardinal decomposition - assigning a share of overall risk to specific named sources - as new in the literature, and applies the same approach to patent texts and job postings
old_way: Answering 'which firms are exposed to this shock, and how much' via ad hoc surveys or an economist's qualitative reading of a sample of disclosures - available with a lag and not comparable across firms or over time.
new_way: A standing classifier scores every listed firm's call sentences for shock-specific exposure each quarter, giving a continuously updating, cross-firm-comparable time series built from firms' own disclosed language.
so_what: When the next shock arrives, the honest answer to 'how exposed are we versus our competitors' does not require commissioning anything - it exists by the following earnings-call cycle, from text that is already public. That collapses the lead time your emerging-risk and market-intelligence functions currently budget for, and it means an outside party can quantify your exposure on the same timetable you can.
verification_note: The NBER abstract page was re-fetched and does NOT carry the three percentages - they appear only in the full paper, so the 37-page PDF was downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF, where 1.43, 0.98 and 9.88 are all confirmed as prose. CORRECTION: the source slice dated the 0.98 percent trade-policy peak loosely to 'the Trump-era trade war'; the paper specifies 2018Q3, which is used here. NBER working papers explicitly state they have not been peer-reviewed, so strength is capped at B. One co-author (Kalyani) is a Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis economist but the paper carries the standard non-institutional disclaimer; treated as independent academic work and deliberately NOT merged with SENSE-03 despite both mining earnings calls, because the signals differ (bank-sector stress convergence versus per-firm shock decomposition) and the evidence grades differ.

finding: In a peer-reviewed Wharton/Cornell study, GPT-4-generated new-product concepts scored higher than Wharton students' concepts on a purchase-intent SURVEY - a stated-intent rating, not sales or adoption - and were seven times more likely to land in the top decile of that rating.
evidence: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave & Ulrich, received January 2026 and accepted July 2026 after two revisions; arXiv:2607.27553 | 100 GPT-4 zero-shot ideas averaged 46.4% purchase intent and 100 few-shot ideas 49.3%, against 40.4% for 200 human ideas; the paper reports AI-generated ideas are 'seven times more likely to fall into the top decile of ideas based on purchase intent' | The outcome measure is a five-point stated purchase-intent scale (definitely would not purchase through definitely would purchase) converted to probabilities using a Jamieson and Bass (1989) weighting, rated by US college-age respondents recruited on Prolific, each evaluating an average of 40 randomised and blinded ideas | A follow-up study rephrasing human ideas in GPT-4's writing style found no significant quality gain (B=0.009, 95% CI [-0.005, 0.023], p=.205), ruling out persuasive phrasing as the driver
old_way: Concept pools sourced from human brainstorming or crowdsourced innovation tournaments, then screened with a purchase-intent instrument before development spend.
new_way: LLM-generated concept pools added to or substituted for the human pool, screened with the same instrument at a fraction of the generation cost.
so_what: Be precise about what this licenses and what it does not. It says an LLM can out-produce your ideation workshop on the screening metric you already use - which means the cost of filling the top of the funnel has collapsed and any stage-gate calibrated to human idea supply is now mis-set. It does NOT say those concepts sell: the measure is what a rater says they would buy, on sub-USD-50 products for college students, using a May 2023 model. Anyone presenting this as evidence of realised revenue is over-reading it, and a sceptical room will find that seam first.
verification_note: 68-page PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF in this run (WebFetch cannot parse the raw stream). 46.4, 49.3, 40.4, the 'seven times more likely' top-decile claim, the Jamieson and Bass weighting, gpt-4-0314, the Prolific recruitment and the B=0.009 rephrasing null are all confirmed in the extracted text, as is the line 'Received: January 2026; accepted: July 2026 by Kalyan Singhal and Subodha Kumar after two revisions'. CORRECTION: the source slice said each idea was rated by about 20 Prolific respondents; that figure could not be located and has been replaced with the verified statement that each respondent evaluated an average of 40 ideas. The journal name is not printed on the fetched preprint (the named handling editors are Production and Operations Management editors) so acceptance is asserted, the venue is not. Authors are Wharton/Cornell faculty under IRB Protocol #853634 with no vendor sponsor. Scope caveat is material: products under USD 50 for college students, gpt-4-0314 prompted in May 2023.

finding: On a real commercial idea-screening platform, adding LLM ratings to a model trained on the firm's own historical expert ratings cut client evaluation effort by up to 28.4%, but the paper attributes only 3.8% of that reduction to the LLM - the rest comes from re-weighting the human expert scores the firm already had.
evidence: Rhodes, Kireyev, Yang & Borah, Research Square preprint rs-7085870 v1, posted 28 August 2025 | Data cover 74,436 idea submissions across 153 ideation contests run for major advertisers over two years on one crowdsourcing platform, each submission rated by several hired internal experts | The paper states the platform 'can reduce client evaluation time by up to 28.4% (holding fixed the platform's workload), of which 3.8% can be attributed to LLM-generated ratings (augmentation effect)' | On headcount, the framework lets the platform 'eliminate any one from a set of 5 experts out of 10, of which 2 additional experts become replaceable thanks to the contribution of LLM' - i.e. 3 of 10 from the machine-learning model on historical human ratings alone, and 2 more only once LLM ratings are added
old_way: Internal experts read and rate every submission before a shortlist reaches the sponsor, so review cost scales linearly with submission volume.
new_way: LLM ratings combined with a model trained on historical expert ratings and actual sponsor choices triage the pool, concentrating expert attention without reducing how many ideas are generated.
so_what: This is the most defensible version of the AI-screening story and it points somewhere uncomfortable for a technology-first roadmap. Once generation is cheap the binding constraint moves to evaluation - but here roughly seven-eighths of the efficiency gain came from finally exploiting the firm's own archive of past expert ratings and sponsor decisions, not from the model. If your organisation has not retained and structured that archive, buying an LLM screener will get you the small part of the benefit. The asset is your decision history.
verification_note: 52-page preprint re-downloaded and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF in this run; the DOI landing page was separately confirmed live at HTTP 200 and is cited as the stable alternative because the assets-eu direct link carries an expiring query parameter. 74,436, 153, 28.4 and 3.8 are all confirmed in the extracted text. TWO CORRECTIONS: the source slice stated the reduction flatly as '28.4%' where the paper's own wording is 'up to 28.4%', and it rendered the LLM share as '3.8 percentage points', where the paper says only '3.8%' - the paper is genuinely ambiguous about whether that is 3.8 points of the 28.4 or 3.8% of it, so the paper's wording is reproduced verbatim rather than resolved. Preprint posted August 2025, not confirmed to have completed peer review, so source_type is RESEARCH_FIRM and strength is capped at B. Authors (INSEAD, LSE, HEC Paris) declare no competing interests in the fetched text. Platform and advertiser clients are unnamed for commercial confidentiality, hence company MULTIPLE. Domain is advertising and product-idea crowdsourcing, NOT financial services - it is not counted toward the finserv target.

finding: In a peer-reviewed Annals of Operations Research study on a retail bank's own customer data, adding account-transaction behaviour to the demographic and product-ownership data that conventional cross-sell propensity models use raised consumer-loan targeting AUC by about 4-5%, and deep-learning features compressed from the raw transactions added a further 0.008.
evidence: Boustani, Emrouznejad, Gholami, Despic & Ioannou, 'Improving the predictive accuracy of the cross-selling of consumer loans using deep learning networks', Annals of Operations Research, accepted 19 January 2023 | Sample is 6,127 individual customers of an unnamed Middle Eastern bank, restricted to those holding at least one credit card and an active account; SMEs and liberal professions excluded | Combining transaction data with demographics and product ownership produced 'a 4% increase of AUC in the case of Random Forests and 5.4% in the case of Gradient Boosting Machine' - in the published Random Forest table this is roughly 0.787 to 0.815 across ensemble sizes | An auto-encoder was used to extract 8 latent features from the transaction data alone; a sixfold cross-validation on those 8 features as the only input produced an AUC of 0.777, and adding them to the best heterogeneous ensemble raised its average AUC from 0.925 to 0.933, which the authors call 'a modest but valuable enhancement'
old_way: Retail cross-sell propensity scored from demographics (age, income, family status) plus flags for products the customer already holds.
new_way: The same propensity model augmented with account-transaction behaviour, plus deep-learning-compressed latent features from that behaviour, to identify which customers are genuine opportunities for a specific product.
so_what: This is what an honest, auditable AI opportunity-identification result in banking looks like, and the size of it is the message. Not a transformation - a few points of AUC from transaction data you already hold, and less than one point from the deep-learning layer on top. Use it two ways in front of a sceptical room: as proof the mechanism is real and checkable, and as the yardstick against which to measure any vendor promising hyper-personalisation uplift an order of magnitude larger without showing you an AUC table.
verification_note: Open-access PDF re-downloaded from Aston's institutional repository and text-extracted locally with PyMuPDF in this run; the repository record page was separately confirmed live at HTTP 200. MAJOR CORRECTION: the source slice reported the lift as '4 percentage points' and '5.4 percentage points' of AUC. The paper says '4% increase of AUC' and '5.4%', which are RELATIVE increases - the Random Forest table moves from about 0.787 to about 0.815, i.e. under 3 points absolute. Presenting these as percentage points would have overstated the result by roughly a third and is exactly the kind of error a sceptical stakeholder finds. The 0.777 auto-encoder-only AUC IS confirmed (Table 9) as is the 0.925 to 0.933 ensemble improvement. Footnote 1 confirms 'For confidentiality, the name of the bank is not revealed'. Under this project's unnamed-institution rule a quantified claim about an unnamed institution would normally be dropped; kept here as a deliberate judgment call because the quantified claim is about a published, reproducible modelling method in a peer-reviewed journal with an academic confidentiality footnote, not an institutional performance claim in a vendor deck - but the caveat is live and is flagged in the cover note. Classical/predictive ML (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, auto-encoder), not generative AI. Vintage: accepted January 2023, i.e. pre-LLM-era technique.

finding: The same LLM idea pools that scored higher on average purchase intent were significantly less diverse as a SET of generated CONCEPTS - a distinct homogenisation problem from the under-dispersion seen in LLM-simulated respondents (SENSE-01), since here the model is producing the options rather than imitating the people judging them.
evidence: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave & Ulrich, arXiv:2607.27553, Studies 2a/2b/3a/3b | Within-set pairwise semantic similarity was significantly higher (i.e. diversity lower) for GPT-4 zero-shot ideas than for human ideas (B=0.193, 95% CI [0.182, 0.204], t(298)=33.89, p<.001) and lower still for few-shot ideas (B=0.207, 95% CI [0.196, 0.219], t(298)=35.98, p<.001); the gap survived rephrasing, retaining 80-90% of its size after style standardisation | Re-analysing three previously published AI-creativity datasets (Stevenson et al. 2022, Hubert et al. 2024, Boussioux et al. 2024), AI-generated ideas were less diverse in every comparison, with effect sizes 'ranging from small (Cohen's d = 0.380) to very large (d = 5.538)' | The loss is partly reversible: pooling across model vendors plus prompt engineering (chain-of-thought, heterogeneous personas or constraints) and agents that explore the solution space raised diversity 'almost to the level of human idea generation', while newer single models alone still fell short of human-level diversity
old_way: Human ideation, where independently generated concepts are naturally dispersed across the opportunity space, so a pool's coverage roughly tracks its size.
new_way: LLM concept pools that score well individually but cluster tightly in semantic space, so adding more AI ideas buys less additional coverage of the opportunity landscape than the count suggests.
so_what: A portfolio built on average idea quality will look better on the scorecard while exploring less of the market. Innovation-tournament economics says the value of a concept set comes from its best idea, which depends on variance and coverage, not the mean - so an LLM-only funnel optimises the metric that does not pay. Two concrete instructions for a portfolio owner: instrument pool diversity, not just mean score, before any stage gate; and if you generate with a single model on a single prompt template you are buying a narrower opportunity space than your predecessor had, at lower cost. The mitigation - multiple vendors, varied prompts - is cheap, but only if someone is measuring.
verification_note: Same locally extracted PDF as IDEATE-01 (accepted July 2026 after two revisions). B=0.193, B=0.207, the d=0.380 to d=5.538 range, the 80-90% survival after style standardisation and the 'almost to the level of human idea generation' mitigation result are all confirmed in the extracted text. Kept as a SEPARATE row from SENSE-01 on explicit instruction and on the merits: SENSE-01 concerns LLMs imitating survey RESPONDENTS and failing at individual-level fidelity, while this concerns LLMs generating CONCEPTS whose set-level variance is compressed. They are different literatures and different failure surfaces even though both are forms of output homogenisation, and collapsing them would obscure that a firm can be hit by both at once - a narrowed concept set screened by a synthetic panel that is itself under-dispersed. The d=0.380 to 5.538 meta-analysis re-analyses three other teams' datasets; those originals were not independently re-fetched, so those effect sizes are as reported by this paper's re-analysis. The headline diversity result rests on the authors' own data in an accepted paper, hence strength A.
